articles.title_original: Lattice composite Fermi liquid with broken inversion symmetry
articles.title_en: Transport Signatures and Non-Analytic Responses in Lattice Composite Fermi Liquids in Rhombohedral Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We study transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids realized in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry. We show that reduced crystalline symmetry exposes intrinsic singular dynamical responses of composite fermions that are otherwise hidden in the conventional Landau-level setting. At zero wave vector, inversion breaking allows gauge-field fluctuations to generate a non-analytic longitudinal optical resistivity, with $\operatorname{Re}ρ^{xx}(ω)\sim |ω|^{4/3}$ for gate-screened Coulomb interactions. At finite wave vector $\mathbf{q}$, inversion breaking leads to nonreciprocal transport and a non-analytic $\sim |\mathbf{q}|$ dependence of the Hall conductivity, both of which can be probed through surface acoustic wave propagation. We also discuss a distinct mechanism for singular DC transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids: renormalization of $2k_F$ scattering at the composite Fermi surface enhances Umklapp relaxation and can lead to a non-analytic temperature dependence of the resistivity. Taken together, our results identify transport signatures of lattice composite Fermi liquids that are absent in their continuum quantum Hall counterparts and can be directly tested in ongoing experiments on twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene, where evidence for zero-field composite Fermi liquids has recently been reported.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates transport phenomena in lattice composite Fermi liquids realized in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry. The authors analyze how reduced crystalline symmetry exposes singular dynamical responses, such as non-analytic optical resistivity and nonreciprocal transport, which can be observed in rhombohedral graphene. These findings provide direct transport signatures for zero-field composite Fermi liquids recently reported in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides and rhombohedral graphene systems.

articles.title_original: Effects of gold cluster intercalation in graphene: stationary waves and modified QPI features
articles.title_en: Effects of gold cluster intercalation in graphene on stationary waves and QPI features
articles.excerpt_original: Gold intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC produces a cluster phase with unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference (QPI) features concentrated near the graphene M points. We show that this can be explained by Au intercalation below graphene hollow sites, which induces a local scattering potential on the six surrounding carbon atoms. Within a T-matrix treatment, this ring-like scatterer produces elliptical QPI structures centered near M, in agreement with the experimental FT-STS measurements. We further show that these QPI features naturally generate the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns observed in real space. Finally, we compute the local-density-of-states contrast on and off a small cluster and show that its sign and magnitude are strongly energy dependent, consistent with the experimental observations.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigate the intercalation of gold clusters beneath epitaxial graphene on silicon carbide, revealing the formation of a cluster phase with unique standing waves and quasiparticle-interference characteristics. Using a T-matrix treatment, the study demonstrates how localized scattering potentials from these intercalated structures generate elliptical QPI features and stationary wave patterns. The calculated local-density-of-states contrast exhibits a strong energy dependence that aligns well with experimental scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements.

articles.title_original: An iterative method bridging DFT, disorder averaging, and experiment in intercalated materials: application to Au-intercalated graphene
articles.title_en: Iterative modeling method for Au-intercalated graphene bridging DFT and experiment
articles.excerpt_original: Intercalation can strongly modify the electronic dispersion of a host material, as directly revealed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). We develop a general iterative method combining density functional theory (DFT), tight-binding (TB), disorder averaging within the self-consistent T-matrix approximation (SCTMA), and experiment, to construct an effective model of the intercalated system. DFT identifies the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom and constrains selected model parameters, while comparison of SCTMA calculations with experiment guides their further refinement. We apply this method to graphene intercalated with Au clusters and show that it reproduces the main ARPES signatures of the Au-cluster phase, including the broadening of the V12an Hove singularity and the emergence of kink-like features in the dispersion. The essential microscopic ingredients identified by the analysis are the hybridization between selected intercalant orbitals and the graphene states, together with an intercalation-induced local scattering potential.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed an iterative modeling approach that combines density functional theory, tight-binding models, disorder averaging, and experimental data to study intercalated 2D materials. Applied to gold-cluster-intercalated graphene, the method successfully reproduces key angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy signatures such as Van Hove singularity broadening and dispersion kinks. This work advances the understanding of hybridization and scattering phenomena in metal-intercalated graphene systems.

articles.title_original: Semi-Dirac semi-metals quantum dots

articles.excerpt_original: Novel findings on nanostructures in semi-metal and semi-graphene materials are discussed regarding rectangular quantum dots with zigzag edges, MIT bag models, and Dirichlet boundary conditions. The article theoretically investigates some models of quantum dots for these hybrid materials and the point spectra of the semi-Dirac semi-Laplacians via one-dimensional Laplace and Dirac operators. We also prove the self-adjointness of the semi-Laplacian defined on a rectangle, subject to zigzag and hard-wall boundary conditions, and study its spectral properties.

articles.title_original: Tunable Conformal Graphene Growth on Oxide Nanotube scaffolds: Towards Superwettable Hierarchical 2D-3D Architectures
articles.title_en: Tunable Conformal Graphene Growth on Oxide Nanotube Scaffolds for Hierarchical 2D-3D Architectures
articles.excerpt_original: Hierarchical hybrid nanoarchitectures that integrate vertically oriented graphene nanowalls, GNWs, with metal oxide, MeOx, nanotube scaffolds offer versatile platform for smart surfaces, nanoelectronics, and electrochemical technologies. Herein we present rapid, dry, plasma-assisted fabrication route that enables direct and conformal growth of GNWs on mechanically robust MeOx nanoforests. The method combines supported single-crystalline organic nanowires as a 1D soft template with sequential plasma-enabled oxide deposition and GNW growth, all performed under mild temperature, power, and vacuum conditions. This approach yields an unprecedented 2D-3D hierarchical architecture consisting of tunable-thickness MeOx nanotubes uniformly decorated with radially oriented graphene nanosheets, forming re-entrant, multiscale surface. Resulting hierarchical roughness imparts fluorine-free, long-term omniphobicity, with contact angles exceeding 170 degree for water, bovine serum, and other complex fluids. GNWs dominate the wetting response across TiO2, Al2O3, and SiO2 nanotube scaffolds, effectively decoupling surface behavior from intrinsic oxide chemistry and maintaining robust repellency under UV irradiation and water condensation. Comprehensive SEM, TEM, XPS, angle-resolved NEXAFS, and Raman analyses elucidate growth mechanism and confirm preservation of the sp2 graphitic framework, together with controlled degree of edge functionalization. Overall, this work establishes universal, substrate-compatible, low-temperature, and scalable route for the fabrication of tunable graphene-metal oxide nano-microstructured multifunctional surfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a rapid, dry, plasma-assisted fabrication route for the direct and conformal growth of vertically oriented graphene nanowalls on metal oxide nanotube scaffolds. The resulting 2D-3D hierarchical architecture achieves fluorine-free, long-term omniphobicity with contact angles exceeding 170 degrees across various complex fluids. This scalable, low-temperature method decouples surface behavior from intrinsic oxide chemistry, offering potential for smart surfaces, nanoelectronics, and electrochemical technologies.

articles.title_original: Probing the Potential Profile of Twisted Bilayer Graphene via Fabry-Pérot Interference
articles.title_en: Probing Potential Profile in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Using Fabry-Pérot Interference
articles.excerpt_original: We use Fabry-Pérot interference to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. We trace anomalous resistance oscillations in the nominally unipolar regime to a hidden cavity formed by unintentional local doping in our device. By analyzing zero-field interference patterns, we determine the location and size of this inhomogeneity. Magnetotransport measurements support the model, distinguishing local cavity modes from global resonances through their different magnetic dependence. Simulations using our extracted profile reproduce the experimental features. Our results highlight interference spectroscopy as a simple, non-invasive probe for identifying local defects and internal potential barriers in ballistic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers utilize Fabry-Pérot interference to investigate the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The study traces anomalous resistance oscillations to an unintentional local doping cavity, demonstrating interference spectroscopy as an effective non-invasive probe for detecting local defects in ballistic devices.

articles.title_original: Trion Excitations in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: A Quantum Monte Carlo Study
articles.title_en: Quantum Monte Carlo Study Reveals Dirac Trions in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Determining the nature of charge carriers is a fundamental goal in the study of strongly correlated electron systems. Here, we employ the continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo method to reveal exotic "Dirac trion" excitations in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. While the ground state is a symmetry-breaking insulator with gapped ($\sim$ 20 meV) electron-like excitations, we show that a small temperature ($\sim$ 3 meV), well below the interaction scale, drives the system into a strongly fluctuating symmetric normal state. We demonstrate that this normal state hosts gapless excitations consisting of three-particle bound states, two electrons and one hole, that are exactly orthogonal to the higher-energy electrons at the zero-momentum gapless point. These Dirac trions have the remarkable property of being arbitrarily light despite being composed of heavy constituents, and their spectra can be easily tuned by varying the twist angle and interlayer hopping strength. Our unbiased quantum many-body computation sheds light on the Dirac trions in a projected correlated flat-band setting and opens the door for further investigation of many-body excitations in strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels.
articles.summary_en: Researchers employed the continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo method to identify gapless three-particle bound states, known as Dirac trions, in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. The study demonstrates that these excitations remain remarkably light despite being composed of heavy constituents and can be tuned via the twist angle and interlayer hopping strength. This theoretical finding advances the understanding of strongly correlated topological bands and many-body excitations.

articles.title_original: Dynamic magnetic properties of graphene/fullerene/graphene sandwich structure based on the Monte Carlo method
articles.title_en: Monte Carlo study of dynamic magnetic properties in graphene/fullerene/graphene sandwich structures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The dynamic magnetic response and hysteresis characteristics of a mixed-spin Ising model constructed on the graphene/fullerene/graphene (G/F/G) sandwich architecture are systematically examined using the Monte Carlo method. By sweeping key intrinsic and extrinsic control parameters, including intra- and inter-layer exchange couplings ( J a , J b , J ab ), single-ion anisotropies ( D a , D b ), and the defining components of the applied magnetic field (amplitude h 0 , period τ , and static bias field h b ), while the rich spectrum of magnetically ordered states is uncovered. The system hosts Néel-type magnetization profiles, exhibits single and double compensation points ( T comp1 , T comp2 ), and undergoes well-defined dynamic phase transitions marked by a critical temperature ( T C ). Constructed phase diagrams map the sensitive dependence of T C and T comp on each parameter, while the dynamic hysteresis loops display pronounced reshaping, area evolution, and positional shifts driven by the interplay between intrinsic relaxation and sublattice-resolved field sensitivity. These findings quantitatively clarify the magnetic tunability of G/F/G heterostructures and offer actionable guidance for designing multi-state spintronic devices.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the dynamic magnetic response and hysteresis characteristics of a mixed-spin Ising model built on a graphene/fullerene/graphene sandwich architecture using the Monte Carlo method. These findings offer theoretical insights into the magnetic tunability of these heterostructures for potential multi-state spintronic device applications.

articles.title_original: On‑Demand Design of High‑Q Metasurfaces via Physics‑Conditioned Closed‑Loop Learning
articles.title_en: On-Demand Design of High-Q Metasurfaces via Physics-Conditioned Closed-Loop Learning
articles.excerpt_original: Accurate modeling of spectral evolution across broad geometric parameter spaces is critical for designing high‑Q metasurfaces based on bound states in the continuum (BICs). However, conventional full‑wave simulations are too slow for practical parameter exploration, and existing deep‑learning models cannot capture both the ultra‑sharp resonances and the dynamic mode‑coupling evolution from bright resonances to hybridized states and quasi‑BICs. Here, we present a physics‑conditioned neural network (PCNN) for high‑Q metasurface design, demonstrated on hexagonal boron nitride metasurfaces that support BICs. The architecture integrates a physics‑constrained front‑end with a feature‑wise linear modulation‑conditioned U‑Net, enabling data‑efficient and high‑fidelity prediction of sharp resonances. An inverse network retrieves structural parameters from target spectra, which are validated through the forward PCNN, closing the computational design loop. We demonstrate accurate modeling and on‑demand designing of hybridized eigenstates, toroidal dipole modes, and quasi‑BICs across wide wavelength ranges (R2 > 0.96). This work provides a unified platform for studying BIC physics and realizing customizable metasurfaces for sensing, nonlinear, and topological photonics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a physics-conditioned neural network for high-Q metasurface design using hexagonal boron nitride. The architecture integrates a physics-constrained front-end with a modulation-conditioned U-Net to predict sharp resonances and enable inverse structural parameter retrieval. This approach offers a unified platform for studying bound states in the continuum and realizing customizable metasurfaces for sensing and photonics applications.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear dynamics and chaotic behavior of curved self-sustaining BNNTs under combined thermal and magnetic fields
articles.title_en: Nonlinear dynamics and chaotic behavior of curved boron nitride nanotubes under thermal and magnetic fields
articles.excerpt_original: This study examines the primary resonance and chaotic vibration behavior of a curved single-walled boron nitride nanotube (CSWBNNT) subjected to axial thermo-magnetic loading and transverse harmonic excitation on a viscoelastic foundation. The system is modeled using nonlocal Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and reduced to an ordinary differential equation via a single-mode Galerkin approximation. The method of multiple scales is applied to derive analytical expressions for the primary resonance response of a clamped–clamped CSWBNNT. Parametric effects, including nonlinear contributions of the viscoelastic medium, sinusoidal curvature amplitudes, and Young’s modulus value, are investigated with emphasis on frequency response, jumping phenomena, and instability regions. Numerical simulations using the Runge–Kutta method generate bifurcation diagrams, phase plane trajectories, and Poincaré maps to characterize periodic and chaotic dynamics. Results reveal that thermo-magnetic forces strongly influence resonance behavior, while chaotic vibrations are highly sensitive to excitation amplitude, underscoring the complex interplay between external loading and nonlinear structural parameters.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the primary resonance and chaotic vibration behavior of a curved single-walled boron nitride nanotube under combined thermal and magnetic loads. Using nonlocal Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and the method of multiple scales, the researchers analyze frequency responses, instability regions, and parametric effects. Numerical simulations reveal that thermo-magnetic forces strongly influence resonance, and chaotic dynamics are sensitive to excitation amplitudes.

articles.title_original: Spin-canting-induced Giant Nonlinear Optical Magnetochirality in a 2D Ferrotoroid
articles.title_en: Giant Nonlinear Optical Magnetochirality Induced by Spin-Canting in 2D CrSBr
articles.excerpt_original: Achieving magnetically switchable chiral light emission is an important goal for 2D opto-spintronics. However, conventional strategies face a fundamental trade-off between dynamic tunability and polarization contrast. Nonlinear optics, particularly the emerging mechanism of chiral second-harmonic generation (SHG), offers a distinct strategy to bypass this restriction, yet its experimental realization remains elusive due to stringent symmetry requirements. Here, we report giant nonlinear optical magnetochirality in a centrosymmetric 2D ferrotoroid, bilayer (2L) CrSBr. We reveal that a field-induced spin-canting state breaks the parity-time (PT) symmetry of the unperturbed antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state, activating a spin-chirality-driven i-type susceptibility. The coherent interference between this emergent i-type and intrinsic c-type SHG susceptibilities generates a macroscopic circularly polarized SHG signal whose helicity is magnetically switchable. Leveraging this sensitive mechanism, we uncover remanent magnetic states after field saturation that evade conventional linear probes. By exploiting the non-volatility of these states, we demonstrate magneto-optical memory and logic operations. Our work establishes a general symmetry-driven strategy for tailoring nonlinear magnetochirality, while providing a sensitive optical probe for subtle spin textures in the 2D limit.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate giant nonlinear optical magnetochirality in a centrosymmetric 2D ferrotoroid, bilayer CrSBr, using a field-induced spin-canting state to break PT symmetry. This mechanism generates a magnetically switchable circularly polarized second-harmonic generation (SHG) signal, enabling non-volatile magneto-optical memory and logic operations. The work establishes a symmetry-driven strategy for tailoring nonlinear magnetochirality and probing subtle spin textures in the 2D limit.

articles.title_original: Drumhead Surface States of Rhombohedral Graphite with Near Ideal Quantum Geometry Condition
articles.title_en: Quantum Geometry and Surface States in Rhombohedral Graphite
articles.excerpt_original: The ideal quantum geometry (IQG) condition of equal magnitude between quantum metric ($G(k)$) and Berry curvature ($Ω(k)$) as in $|Ω|$/Tr$G$=1 has been associated with realizing fractional Chern insulators for the flat band in few layers of rhombohedral graphene (RG). More recently the IQG condition has also been proposed for superconductivity in the flat band for thick RG layers. Using density functional theory and Wannier functions, we study the symmetry-protected topology of bulk RG, drumhead surface state (DSS) of semi-infinite RG surface, and the IQG condition for thick RG slabs. We find that bulk RG is a weak topological insulator with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), besides being effectively a chiral semimetal with chiral nodal line without SOC. We also find that the DSS flat band of semi-infinite and thick RG slabs have a sizable convex curvature with depth agreeing with the recent angular resolved phono-emission spectroscopy experiment. The calculated IQG also shows a convex shape with the K point at the center having a minimum with approximately $|Ω|$/Tr$G$$\approx$1. But the inner rim of the DSS region shows the strict IQG condition of $|Ω|$/Tr$G$=1. These results on semi-infinite and thick RG slabs from first-principles calculations provide useful information for the pristine DSS at the single particle level for future studies to consider when many-body interactions and strong correlations will be included.
articles.summary_en: Researchers utilize density functional theory and Wannier functions to study the symmetry-protected topology, drumhead surface states, and ideal quantum geometry condition of rhombohedral graphite. The study demonstrates that bulk rhombohedral graphite functions as a weak topological insulator with spin-orbit coupling, providing foundational single-particle insights for future investigations into many-body interactions and strong correlations.

The ability of peripheral nerves to spontaneously repair small injuries is limited, necessitating complex surgical grafts with secondary complications in larger cases. This research develops a revolutionary strategy based on hybrid nanobridges made from a scientifically proven combination of graphene (59%) and boron nitride (41%). Graphene provides ultrafast electrical conductivity (1.6 × 10⁶ m/s), while boron nitride ensures optimal biocompatibility (9.4/10) and mechanical stability. The results revealed that the optimal hybrid ratio increased the efficiency of nerve signal transmission by 40%, and increased the quantum tunneling probability to 0.65 at 3 nm, accelerating axonal regeneration. The high electric field concentration (0.1 V/nm) in the nucleus allows for precise stimulation of damaged cells. By combining the superior electrochemical properties of graphene with the optimal biocompatibility of boron nitride, these nanobridges represent a quantum leap in neural tissue engineering, opening new horizons for treating spinal paralysis and complex injuries.

articles.title_en: Review on Graphene- and Fullerene-Based Heterocyclic Conducting Polymers
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene and fullerene derivatives are highly promising carbon-based nanomaterials, with superior electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties, making them prime materials for constructing sophisticated conducting polymers. When combined with heterocyclic compounds such as polythiophenes, polypyrroles, and polyanilines, these materials exhibit synergistic properties, including improved charge transport, structural stability, and resistance to external environments. This review provides a thorough overview of composites, recent advances in materials science, and the synthesis, structural modulation, and functionalization of graphene- and fullerene-based heterocyclic conductive polymers. It also focuses on interfacial interactions, doping mechanisms, and morphological factors controlling their optoelectronic and electrochemical performance. The study also discusses their multifaceted applications in energy storage devices, sensors, flexible electronics, and organic photovoltaics. The main challenges, including dispersion uniformity, polymer-nanocarbon compatibility, and scalable fabrication, are critically evaluated. At the end, by consolidating existing knowledge and demarking directions for future work, this review is intended to facilitate continued innovation in hybrid organic-inorganic electronic materials.
articles.summary_en: This academic review explores the synthesis, structural modulation, and functionalization of graphene- and fullerene-based heterocyclic conductive polymers. It details interfacial interactions, doping mechanisms, and performance factors for applications in energy storage, sensors, and flexible electronics. The study also critically evaluates key challenges such as dispersion uniformity and scalable fabrication.

articles.title_original: Magnetic Breakdown and Anomalous Quantum Oscillation in Rhombohedral Tetralayer Graphene
articles.title_en: Magnetic Breakdown and Anomalous Quantum Oscillations in Rhombohedral Tetralayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate magnetic breakdown near Van Hove singularities (VHSs) in the electron-doped rhombohedral tetralayer graphene, where chiral superconductivity has recently been reported. Using the noninteracting band structure and Kubo formula, we identify anomalous Shubnikov-de Haas effects: Ring-like structures in the Landau fan and anomalous high-frequency peaks in the frequency spectra. These anomalous quantum oscillations can be understood by the reconstruction from magnetic breakdown among three nearby Fermi pockets separated by VHSs. Remarkably, these qualitative anomalous features persist into a stronger-VHS regime, where the semiclassical picture breaks down. The temperature and (weak) disorder dependence of the oscillations are also investigated. Our results establish that the magnetic-breakdown-induced anomalous quantum oscillation provides a general distinctive probe for the underlying Fermi-surface geometry associated with VHSs and may explain the recent quantum oscillation experiment in rhombohedral tetralayer graphene [arXiv:2606.05356].
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigate magnetic breakdown near Van Hove singularities in electron-doped rhombohedral tetralayer graphene using noninteracting band structures and the Kubo formula. The study identifies anomalous Shubnikov-de Haas effects and ring-like structures in the Landau fan, providing insight into the underlying Fermi-surface geometry associated with chiral superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Scanning Gate Microscopy Modulation of Supercurrent in Graphene Josephson Junctions
articles.title_en: Scanning Gate Microscopy Modulation of Supercurrent in Graphene Josephson Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene Josephson junctions represent an excellent platform for quantum technologies, thanks to the combination of high carrier mobility, ballistic transport, and large gate-tunable critical currents, preserved even under quantizing magnetic fields. Investigating the spatial distribution of supercurrent flow could be crucial for elucidating transport mechanisms and advancing the engineering of these devices. In this work, we employ a Scanning Gate Microscope to investigate supercurrent transport in hBN-encapsulated graphene Josephson junctions contacted by Niobium leads. We study the supercurrent modulation as a function of the applied tip voltage bias and tip-to-sample distance, and provide a complete characterization of the tip-induced modulation. Our experimental results are quantitatively consistent with numerical simulations and pave the way towards local mapping and manipulation of gate-tunable superconducting phenomena with unprecedented spatial resolution.
articles.summary_en: Researchers utilize a scanning gate microscope to investigate supercurrent transport in hBN-encapsulated graphene Josephson junctions with niobium contacts. The study details supercurrent modulation based on tip voltage bias and distance, yielding results that match numerical simulations. This work enables the local mapping and manipulation of gate-tunable superconducting phenomena for quantum technologies.

articles.title_original: Andreev reflection in graphene–superconductor junctions with line defects
articles.title_en: Andreev reflection and valley-dependent transport in graphene-superconductor junctions with line defects
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate Andreev reflection and valley-dependent transport in a graphene/line-defect/superconductor junction. Using a tight-binding model combined with the Bogoliubov–de Gennes formalism and a scattering matrix approach, we show that the line defect acts as a universal valley filter for both electrons and holes, independent of their band index. This universal behavior originates from the invariance of the pseudospin structure governing transmission across conduction and valence bands. Based on this property, we identify two distinct transport mechanisms associated with different Andreev reflection regimes. In the retro-Andreev reflection regime, where electrons and holes reside in the same band, the defect induces a double-filtering mechanism that enhances valley selectivity and produces strongly asymmetric angular distributions. In contrast, in the specular regime, the interband nature of Andreev reflection leads to a complementary filtering mechanism, which suppresses transport at large incident angles and restores angular symmetry. These features are quantitatively captured by an analytical equation for coherent multiple scattering, which accurately reproduces the zero-bias differential conductance. Our results establish a direct connection between microscopic valley filtering and macroscopic transport observables, demonstrating that differential conductance measurements provide a clear signature of both the Andreev reflection regime and the efficiency of valley filtering.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates Andreev reflection and valley-dependent transport within a graphene, line-defect, and superconductor junction using a tight-binding model and the Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism. The research reveals that the line defect acts as a universal valley filter for both electrons and holes, operating independently of their band index due to pseudospin invariance. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates how distinct retro and specular Andreev reflection regimes influence macroscopic transport observables such as zero-bias differential conductance.

articles.title_original: Emerging Janus TiVC MXene for Thermoelectric Applications
articles.title_en: First-Principles Study Investigates Janus TiVC MXene for Thermoelectric Applications
articles.excerpt_original: A detailed first‐principles study is performed to systematically examine electronic, mechanical, and thermoelectric behavior of Janus TiVC MXene. It exhibits metallic character, while the absence of imaginary phonon frequencies and the negative cohesive energy (−3.68 eV/atom) indicate strong dynamic stability. The thermal stability of the material was evaluated through ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) at 300 and 800 K, which inherently account for anharmonic vibrational effects. Elastic‐constant analysis and strain‐energy fitting reveal high in‐plane stiffness, moderate Poisson's ratio, and robust structural stability, confirming the ability of TiVC MXene to withstand anisotropic loading conditions. Thermoelectric transport properties, explored using the Boltzmann transport formalism, show an improved Seebeck coefficient, high electrical conductivity, and a competitive power factor across a wide temperature range. Such favorable balance between Seebeck coefficient and reduced total thermal conductivity boosts the figure of merit ( ZT ), thereby positioning the Janus TiVC MXene serves as a promising platform for high‐temperature thermoelectric devices.
articles.summary_en: A recent academic study utilizes first-principles calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics to analyze the structural, electronic, mechanical, and thermoelectric properties of Janus TiVC MXene. The material demonstrates high in-plane stiffness, robust dynamic and thermal stability up to 800 K, and favorable thermoelectric transport characteristics. These combined properties yield an improved figure of merit, positioning the material as a promising candidate for high-temperature thermoelectric devices.

articles.title_original: Molten-salt-etched Mo2VC2Tz MXene for zinc-ion supercapacitors
articles.title_en: Molten-salt-etched Mo2VC2Tz MXene for zinc-ion supercapacitors
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the application of molten-salt-etched Mo2VC2Tz MXene materials for high-performance zinc-ion supercapacitors. The research evaluates the electrochemical properties and structural advantages of the synthesized MXene electrodes. Findings contribute to the ongoing development of advanced energy storage systems utilizing transition metal carbides and carbonitrides.

articles.title_original: Solvation Structure Regulated Intercalation Chemistry Enables Scalable and Oxidation‐Suppressed Monolayer MXenes
articles.title_en: Solvation Structure Regulated Intercalation Chemistry Enables Scalable and Oxidation-Suppressed Monolayer MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The scalable production of high‐quality monolayer MXenes is essential but remains challenging due to a persistent yield–quality dilemma during ion intercalation. Conventional hydrated lithium ions ([Li + (H 2 O) x ]) provide insufficient steric expansion to overcome interlayer interactions, resulting in limited monolayer yields, while the water molecules inevitably induce surface oxidation and compromise material quality. Herein, we report a universal Li + solvation structure regulation strategy to address this limitation. By leveraging the strong coordination of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to displace water, the enlarged and water‐deficient ([Li + (DMSO) x (H 2 O) y ]) supramolecular clusters are constructed. The tailored solvation structure simultaneously expands interlayer spacing and forms a hydrophobic interfacial barrier via electron‐transfer‐induced DMSO chemisorption, enabling a high monolayer yield of 95.4% while effectively suppressing oxidation. Importantly, this scalable protocol (100 g scale) exhibits broad applicability to challenging MAX precursors (e.g., Ti 3 AlCN and Ti 2 AlC), enabling the mass production of diverse oxidation‐resistant MXenes. The resulting films show excellent environmental stability and reliable performance in electromagnetic‐interference shielding and infrared thermal camouflage.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a universal lithium-ion solvation structure regulation strategy using dimethyl sulfoxide to suppress oxidation and achieve high monolayer yields of MXenes at a 100-gram scale. The resulting oxidation-resistant MXene films demonstrate excellent environmental stability and performance in electromagnetic-interference shielding and infrared thermal camouflage. This scalable intercalation chemistry addresses the traditional yield-quality dilemma in MXene production.

articles.title_original: Ultra-stable waveguides for on-chip integration of hBN emitters
articles.title_en: Ultra-stable waveguides for on-chip integration of hBN emitters
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Integrating a quantum light source with photonic circuits is crucial for reliable quantum photonics. Layered hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has gained considerable interest as an excellent room-temperature quantum light emitter. However, high-temperature (> 900 °C) thermal annealing is generally necessary to create defect emission in layered hBN, which poses a great challenge for photonic integration. Here, we report ultra-stable optical waveguides (Type T) fabricated by ultrafast laser direct writing within glass. The laser-induced local densification relying on the temperature gradient and pressure wave propagation, endows waveguides with ultra-high stability against high-temperature up to 1100 °C, which provides a fascinating platform for integration of hBN emitters. We develop a waveguide/hBN butt-coupling integrated device. Efficient emissive defects are created in the integrated hBN with single pulse ultrafast laser irradiation a and the subsequent high temperature annealing at 950 °C, and the emission can propagate through the waveguide due to the strong coupling between waveguide and hBN. These findings present a promising pathway towards scalable photonic chips for applications in integrated quantum photonics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report ultra-stable optical waveguides fabricated by ultrafast laser direct writing within glass, capable of withstanding high-temperature annealing up to 1100 °C. This thermal stability enables the successful integration and coupling of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) quantum light emitters for scalable photonic chips. The findings provide a promising pathway for advanced semiconductor and integrated quantum photonics applications.

articles.title_original: Intelligent multi-functional h-BN/ZIF-8 nanocontainers for high-performance anti-corrosion coatings
articles.title_en: Intelligent multi-functional h-BN/ZIF-8 nanocontainers for high-performance anti-corrosion coatings
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the development of intelligent, multi-functional hexagonal boron nitride and ZIF-8 nanocontainers designed for advanced anti-corrosion coating applications. The research highlights improved protective performance and functionality for material surface treatments. Overall, the findings contribute to novel coating formulations utilizing non-graphene 2D and metal-organic framework materials.

articles.title_original: Orbital-DrivenInterfacial Coupling in 2D Ferroelectricvan der Waals Metal–Semiconductor Junctions: A Route to Near-Quantum-LimitContact Resistance
articles.title_en: Orbital-Driven Interfacial Coupling in 2D Ferroelectric van der Waals Metal-Semiconductor Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract van der Waals (vdW) metal–semiconductor junctions (MSJs) are promising for two-dimensional (2D) field-effect transistors, but efficient carrier injection is hindered by tunneling barriers arising from weak interfacial coupling. Here, we propose a strategy to achieve near-quantum-limit contacts by introducing strong interlayer interactions in vdW MSJs, combining bilayer MTe2 (M = Ni, Pd, Pt) electrodes with ferroelectric semiconductors. Confirmed by crystal orbital bond index and crystal orbital Hamilton population analyses, the vertically extended Te-pz orbitals of MTe2 facilitate pz-pz mixing across the interface, forming significant interfacial coupling that enhances tunneling efficiency up to 36.1% while preserving weak Fermi-level pinning (FLP). Under the synergistic effect of ferroelectric-tunable Schottky barriers, ultralow contact resistance down to 51.3 Ω·μm is achieved, approaching the quantum limit. This work highlights the pivotal role of orbital-driven coupling in optimizing vdW contacts, providing a foundational route toward FLP-suppressed low-resistance MSJs for next-generation nanoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a strategy to achieve near-quantum-limit contact resistance in two-dimensional van der Waals metal-semiconductor junctions by introducing strong interlayer interactions and ferroelectric-tunable Schottky barriers. Using bilayer MTe2 electrodes combined with ferroelectric semiconductors, the vertically extended Te-pz orbitals facilitate significant interfacial coupling that enhances tunneling efficiency. This approach reduces contact resistance down to 51.3 ohms-micrometer while preserving weak Fermi-level pinning, offering a pathway toward advanced nanoelectronics.

articles.title_original: Selective Polarity Control of Metal Oxide Semiconductors for Complementary Logic Gates
articles.title_en: Selective Polarity Control of Metal Oxide Semiconductors for Complementary Logic Gates
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Realizing tunable charge carrier polarity is essential for programmable complementary logic circuits. While two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductors have demonstrated polarity controllability through Schottky barrier modulation or contact engineering, their high interfacial sensitivity limits scalability and integration. Here, we present a robust polarity‐conversion strategy for tin oxide (SnO) semiconductors based on electrolyte‐gated transistors (EGTs). In situ electrochemical doping enables the conversion of p‐type SnO to n‐type SnO 2 via Sn 2+ to Sn 4+ oxidation. Both p‐ and n‐type EGTs exhibit outstanding electrical characteristics, including low‐voltage operation, high ON/OFF current ratios, sharp switching behavior, and reliable long‐term stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate the monolithic integration of complementary logic gates, including inverter, NAND, and NOR gates, through spatially selective electrochemical doping of a single SnO layer. Overall, this work provides a scalable and versatile pathway toward oxide‐based programmable complementary circuits.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a robust polarity-conversion strategy for tin oxide semiconductors utilizing electrolyte-gated transistors for programmable complementary logic circuits. In situ electrochemical doping enables the conversion of p-type SnO to n-type SnO2 via oxidation, allowing the monolithic integration of complementary logic gates such as inverters, NAND, and NOR gates. This approach provides a scalable pathway toward advanced oxide-based integrated circuits.

articles.title_original: Growth of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Ribbon Arrays via Droplet Motion Method
articles.title_en: Growth of Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Ribbon Arrays via Droplet Motion Method
articles.excerpt_original: The controlled synthesis of transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) ribbon arrays represents a promising route toward integrating 2D semiconductors into large-scale circuits. However, in ribbon synthesis, excessively large diameters of transition metal source droplets lead to a dominant non-directional surface driving force, which disrupts directional droplet migration and consequently hinders the growth of ribbon arrays. In this work, we leverage the surface energy difference to provide a driving force for the molten precursor droplets, while the atomic steps of the sapphire substrate impart directionality to this force. The introduction of Ni substantially reduced the droplet size, which significantly enhanced the efficacy of this directional driving force. Based on this approach, we successfully guided the directional migration of molten transition metal precursor droplets, thereby enabling the fabrication of highly aligned ribbon arrays. In situ visual chemical vapor deposition enables in situ observation of droplet-mediated growth, while density functional theory calculations and force analyses elucidate the underlying driving mechanisms. This work provides both a mechanistic framework and a versatile synthesis strategy for the scalable fabrication of well-aligned TMD ribbon arrays suitable for next-generation 2D semiconductor integration.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a droplet motion method utilizing surface energy differences and sapphire substrates to synthesize aligned transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) ribbon arrays. The addition of nickel reduced precursor droplet sizes, enhancing directional migration for scalable 2D semiconductor fabrication. This study combines in situ chemical vapor deposition observation and density functional theory calculations to elucidate the underlying growth mechanisms.

articles.title_original: Revisitingthe Schottky-MottRelation for Metal/TransitionMetal Dichalcogenide Interfaces: The Role of Interface Dipoles
articles.title_en: Revisiting the Schottky-Mott Relation for Metal/Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract High contact resistance, stemming from Fermi-level pinning (FLP), is a bottleneck in the contact engineering of transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD)-based two-dimensional field-effect transistors (2DFETs). Our study re-examines the nature of FLP in 2D semiconductors, focusing on regimes where the material thickness is commensurate with the interface thickness. By combining first-principles calculations with experimental validation via ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), we establish the metal effective work function (eWF) as a figure of merit for substantiating the Schottky-Mott relation. Our findings indicate that FLP is governed by both long-range dipole interactions and extended short-range Lennard-Jones potentials. This framework, in conjunction with the linear Schottky-Mott relation, improves predictive capabilities in contact engineering.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates Fermi-level pinning and contact resistance in transition metal dichalcogenide-based two-dimensional field-effect transistors. By combining first-principles calculations with ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy, the researchers demonstrate that interface dipoles govern contact behavior. The findings refine the Schottky-Mott relation to improve predictive capabilities in semiconductor contact engineering.

articles.title_original: Fundamental Theoretical Difference in Ground‐State Spectra of 2‐Electron Systems Bound by Coulomb and Harmonic Potentials
articles.title_en: Fundamental Theoretical Differences in Ground-State Spectra of Two-Electron Systems
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT We note a fundamental difference in the theoretically obtained ground‐state spectra of 2‐electron systems bound by the Coulomb and Harmonic potentials. The Coulomb bound systems considered are the natural Helium atom, Hydrogen molecule, and Tri Hydrogen cation. The “artificial” Harmonic bound systems are the 2D semiconductor quantum dot in a magnetic field with the electron spin moment and its interaction with the magnetic field considered, 3D Hooke's atom, 3D Hooke's molecule, and 3D Tri Harmonic Oscillator cation. Experiment and theory confirm the ground state of natural systems is solely a singlet state. We prove that for the “artificial” systems in the Wigner high‐electron‐correlation regime, there is associated with the ground singlet state, a ground triplet state identified by its replication of theoretical ground state characteristics of correlated systems. The proof is via exact, analytical, correlated wave function solutions of the corresponding Schrödinger‐Pauli/Schrödinger equations for both the ground singlet and triplet states.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the fundamental theoretical differences in ground-state spectra between natural two-electron systems bound by Coulomb potentials and artificial systems bound by harmonic potentials. Using exact analytical solutions of the Schrödinger-Pauli equations, the research demonstrates that artificial systems in the Wigner high-electron-correlation regime feature a ground triplet state associated with the ground singlet state, unlike natural systems which solely exhibit a singlet state.

articles.title_original: Tunable temperature coefficient of resistance in PdSe2 films enabled by strain engineering
articles.title_en: Strain-Engineered Tunable Temperature Coefficient of Resistance in PdSe2 Films for Flexible Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, owing to their exceptional physical properties, show tremendous promise for developing high-performance bolometers and temperature sensors. Yet the temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR), the figure of merit that dictates the sensitivity of such thermosensitive devices, is typically fixed once the material is synthesized, precluding post-fabrication optimization for specific applications. Herein, we demonstrate that the TCR of PdSe 2 can be continuously and reversibly tuned in both directions through strain engineering. Under compressive strain the bandgap widens, whereas it narrows under tensile strain. This band structure reconfiguration translates directly into a controllable shift in TCR. Flexible PdSe 2 sensors fabricated on plastic substrates exhibit exceptionally wide TCR tunability: a modest − 0.63% compressive strain boosts the TCR value by 24.3% (from − 3.7% to − 4.6% °C − 1 ), while 0.56% tensile strain suppresses it by 18.9% (from − 3.7% down to − 3.0% °C − 1 ). Such excellent TCR tunability, together with the advantages of low-temperature and large-area fabrication, makes the PdSe 2 films highly promising for developing reconfigurable electronic skins, adaptive temperature sensors, and next-generation smart wearable sensing devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that the temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) in two-dimensional PdSe2 semiconductor films can be continuously and reversibly tuned using strain engineering. Compressive and tensile strains successfully reconfigure the band structure, leading to controllable shifts in TCR values for flexible sensor applications. This approach enables post-fabrication optimization of thermosensitive devices such as wearable temperature sensors and electronic skins.

articles.title_original: Halogen‐Mediated Polymer‐Free Recovery of Pristine MoS <sub>2</sub> Monolayers From Gold‐Assisted Exfoliation
articles.title_en: Halogen-Mediated Polymer-Free Recovery of Pristine MoS2 Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Metal‐assisted mechanical exfoliation has recently emerged as a powerful strategy for producing large‐area monolayers of two‐dimensional (2D) transition‐metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with near‐intrinsic crystalline quality. The strong adhesion between the TMD monolayer and the metallic adhesion layer poses a significant challenge for device integration, as it generally requires polymer‐assisted transfer processes that introduce contamination, mechanical strain, and structural defects. Here we report a halogen‐mediated biphasic etching strategy that enables the polymer‐free recovery of TMD monolayers directly from gold‐assisted exfoliation substrates. Sequential iodine vapor exposure followed by liquid‐phase iodine etching weakens the Au‐TMD interfacial interaction and subsequently removes the gold adhesion layer while preserving the structural integrity of the monolayer. Spectroscopic characterization, time‐resolved morphological analysis, and first‐principles calculations reveal that iodine adsorption modifies the electronic structure of the Au surface and reduces its binding strength to the TMD layer. MoS 2 monolayers recovered using this approach exhibit significantly reduced strain, lower charge doping, and suppressed wrinkle formation compared with polymer‐transferred counterparts. Optoelectronic devices fabricated from these monolayers demonstrate enhanced photocurrent and improved operational stability. These findings establish halogen‐mediated biphasic etching as a scalable route for integrating pristine 2D semiconductors with technologically relevant substrates and provide a promising pathway toward high‐performance 2D optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a halogen-mediated biphasic etching strategy utilizing iodine vapor and liquid-phase exposure to enable the polymer-free recovery of transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers from gold-assisted exfoliation substrates. This approach weakens the metal-TMD interfacial interaction and removes the gold adhesion layer while preserving structural integrity. The resulting MoS2 monolayers show reduced strain, lower charge doping, and enhanced optoelectronic device performance.

articles.title_original: Te/Fe3GaTe2 1D-2D Ferroelectric Heterojunction Transistors Enabling Ultrafast Multi-State Switching for Workpiece Surface Defect Inspection
articles.title_en: Te/Fe3GaTe2 1D-2D Ferroelectric Heterojunction Transistors for Ultrafast Switching and Defect Inspection
articles.excerpt_original: Ferroelectric field-effect transistors, which rely on ferroelectric polarization reversal to modulate the channel resistance, hold great promise for nonvolatile memory and neuromorphic computing. The polarization switching dynamics are critical for achieving high-speed, high-bit-density neuromorphic hardware. Here, we report a 1D-2D asymmetric heterojunction composed of a single-element tellurium (Te) nanowire and a magnetic metal, Fe3GaTe2. Piezoresponse force microscopy reveals reversible polarization switching at room temperature. Utilizing this ferroelectric heterojunction, we construct ferroelectric semiconductor field-effect transistors that exhibit tunable resistance states exceeding 7 bits, featuring an on/off ratio of 103, a retention time exceeding 103 s, and ultrafast switching down to 20 ns. Moreover, the transistor enables accurate recognition of six kinds of micro-defects with an accuracy of 97.1% on the workpiece surface by convolutional neural network. This work establishes the intrinsic relationship between ferroelectric polarization and resistance modulation, providing a device platform for next-generation multilevel storage and ultrafast neuromorphic computing networks.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a 1D-2D asymmetric ferroelectric heterojunction combining a tellurium nanowire and Fe3GaTe2. The resulting field-effect transistors demonstrate tunable multi-state resistance, ultrafast switching speeds, and high-accuracy workpiece defect recognition using a convolutional neural network. This work advances devices for multilevel nonvolatile storage and neuromorphic computing.

articles.title_original: Interface Barrier Technologies in Advanced Semiconductor Interconnect Metals and Their Reliability Impact: The Evolution from Cu to Co/Ru
articles.title_en: Review of Interface Barrier Technologies and Graphene Encapsulation in Advanced Semiconductor Interconnects
articles.excerpt_original: In the sub-10 nm regime of interconnect, as the dimensions between the backends are becoming smaller, a coupled electrical, reliability, and manufacturability crisis is experienced with the traditional Cu/low-k dual-damascene platform, which is based on a Ta/TaN barrier, a liner stack and a Cu conductor. It is not only the resistivity size effect of Cu alone that functions as a bottleneck, but also the harsh loss of effective conducting cross-section to high-resistivity barrier/liner layers, the reinforcement of interface scattering, and the attendant increase in risks of electromigration, time-dependent dielectric breakdown and thermomechanical failure. This paper reviews the evolution of interface barrier technologies in advanced interconnects, examines the scaling limits of the conventional Cu/Ta (TaN) scheme, and analyzes representative routes including Co-W, Ru-Ta, atomically thin 2D materials, graphene encapsulation, Co-Ti single barrier/liner layers, Ru-Zn self-forming barriers, and Ru semi-damascene integration. The central argument is that the competition in advanced interconnects has shifted from simply identifying the metal with the lowest bulk resistivity to co-designing low-size-effect metals, ultrathin functional interfaces, and new integration architectures to minimize effective line resistance while maximizing reliability. Interface barriers are therefore no longer passive diffusion blockers; they are the functional layers that will decide whether post-Cu interconnect technologies can be industrialized.
articles.summary_en: This academic paper reviews the scaling limits of traditional copper-based interconnects in the sub-10 nm regime and evaluates alternative strategies such as atomically thin 2D materials and graphene encapsulation. It analyzes how interface barriers and low-size-effect metals must be co-designed to minimize line resistance and improve reliability. The study highlights the critical functional role of advanced barrier technologies in enabling post-copper semiconductor industrialization.

articles.title_original: Multistate Control in 2D CuCrP2S6/Sc2CO2 Multiferroic Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Multistate Control in 2D CuCrP2S6/Sc2CO2 Multiferroic Heterostructures for Spintronic Devices
articles.excerpt_original: The magnetoelectric (ME) coupling effect enables effective cross-control between electric and magnetic fields, providing a crucial pathway toward next-generation low-power electronic devices. Here, we propose a two-dimensional (2D) multistate multiferroic heterostructure (MMH) composed of out-of-plane polarized CuCrP2S6 and Sc2CO2 (CCPS/SCO) to realize electric field driven multistate spintronic devices. First-principles calculations demonstrate that the CCPS/SCO heterostructure can be reversibly switched among four non-volatile polarization states (↑↑, ↑↓, ↓↓, ↓↑) using electrical pulses, enabling simultaneous control of electronic transport, magnetic ordering, and spin orientation within a single heterostructure. By encoding the four polarization states, three distinct quantum phases are identified, i.e., out of plane antiferromagnetic metal, in plane ferromagnetic semiconductor and out of plane ferromagnetic metal. The microscopic mechanism underlying this strong ME coupling originates from polarization induced interfacial charge transfer and symmetry breaking, which synergistically shift the energy level and tune the orbital occupation of Cr-d orbitals. Our proposed CCPS/SCO MMH heterostructure establish a promising platform for high-density, low-power, and functionally reconfigurable spintronic memory.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a two-dimensional multistate multiferroic heterostructure composed of CuCrP2S6 and Sc2CO2 to achieve electric field-driven multistate spintronic devices. First-principles calculations demonstrate four reversibly switchable non-volatile polarization states that enable simultaneous control of electronic transport, magnetic ordering, and spin orientation. This strong magnetoelectric coupling originates from polarization-induced interfacial charge transfer and symmetry breaking, offering a platform for reconfigurable spintronic memory.

articles.title_original: Electrically Activating and Switching the Magneto-Optic Faraday Effect in 2D Antiferromagnets
articles.title_en: Electrically Activating and Switching the Magneto-Optic Faraday Effect in 2D Antiferromagnets
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) antiferromagnets are highly promising for next-generation spintronics due to their ultrafast dynamics and robustness against stray fields; however, their practical application is severely hindered by the vanishing magneto-optic effects restricted by strict crystal symmetries. In this work, we propose a universal physical mechanism to activate and manipulate the magneto-optic Faraday effect in 2D fully compensated bilayer antiferromagnets using an external vertical electric field. By constructing a comprehensive tight-binding model and performing first-principles calculations on bilayer VSe2, we demonstrate that the applied electric field explicitly breaks the spatial inversion and combined PT symmetries. This symmetry breaking lifts the Kramers degeneracy, inducing a pronounced spin splitting that, in conjunction with intrinsic spin–orbit coupling, generates non-vanishing Berry curvature. Consequently, the previously forbidden Faraday rotation angle is activated from zero to a significant non-zero value, and its rotation direction can be deterministically reversed by switching the electric field polarity. Our findings provide profound physical insights into the symmetry-modulated light–matter interactions and pave the way for designing fully electrically controllable, energy-efficient antiferromagnetic opto-spintronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a universal physical mechanism to activate and manipulate the magneto-optic Faraday effect in two-dimensional antiferromagnets using an external vertical electric field. By breaking spatial inversion and PT symmetries in bilayer VSe2, the applied field induces spin splitting and generates non-vanishing Berry curvature, enabling electrically controllable Faraday rotation. This work advances energy-efficient antiferromagnetic opto-spintronic device designs.

articles.title_original: Thermal Management and Hot Carrier Multiplication in Few Layered PtSe <sub>2</sub> Devices
articles.title_en: Thermal Management and Hot Carrier Multiplication in Few-Layer PtSe2 Devices
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Engineering of two‐dimensional (2D) material‐based devices for optimize thermal transport and high current carrying capacity has become a prominent research area toward the development of high‐performance next‐generation 2D heterogeneous electronics. In this context, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have gained significant attention due to their tunable physical properties, particularly in relation to electron–phonon interactions and thermal transport mechanisms. Among these, PtSe 2 exhibits a tunable electronic structure from semimetal in bulk to semiconductor at the monolayer limit. This study investigates few layered PtSe 2 ‐based devices to understand their high electric field breakdown behavior and underlying heat dissipation mechanisms at low and room temperatures. The heat dissipation is quantitatively analyzed through the interfacial thermal conductivity measurements of PtSe 2 /SiO 2 and PtSe 2 /h‐BN interfaces with corresponding values as 14.2 MW.m −2 .K −1 and 30.5 MW.m −2 .K −1 , respectively, using Raman thermometry. Electrical breakdown of the devices at room‐temperature is primarily driven by self‐heating effects. A detailed magneto‐transport of PtSe 2 Hall bar devices at low temperatures reveals the carrier multiplication in PtSe 2 under high electric fields as the key contributor causing the superlinear current response and the eventual electrical breakdown of the devices.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates thermal transport, heat dissipation, and hot carrier multiplication in few-layer platinum diselenide (PtSe2) devices. Using Raman thermometry, the researchers quantified interfacial thermal conductivities at PtSe2/SiO2 and PtSe2/h-BN interfaces. The findings provide insights into self-heating effects and electrical breakdown behaviors relevant to next-generation two-dimensional electronics.

articles.title_original: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for 2D Plane Wave Scattering in Arbitrary Dielectric Structures
articles.title_en: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Electromagnetic Wave Scattering in Dielectric Structures
articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, we introduce a meshless physics-informed neural network based computational framework for solving two-dimensional electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media. The framework embeds frequency-domain Maxwell equations and radiation boundary conditions directly into the neural network loss function, enabling accurate prediction of scattered fields for both transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE) polarizations across various dielectric configurations. Application of the method to single-cylinder, concentric multilayer cylindrical shells, three arbitrarily arranged cylinders, and composite irregular structures demonstrates that for the TM polarization, all relative $L^{2}$ errors mostly remain at particularly low levels of $\le0.1$. For the TE polarization, sharp variations of the dielectric properties of scatterers lead to singularities in the governing equations, which result in decreased accuracy of the method. This challenge is overcome by introducing at dielectric boundaries a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function. This procedure significantly improves the accuracy of the method, with the corresponding results closely matching the predictions of the finite-difference time-domain method. This framework exhibits stable convergence behavior across all of the investigated configurations, thus confirming its robustness and scalability to complex electromagnetic scattering problems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a meshless physics-informed neural network framework to solve two-dimensional electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media. By embedding frequency-domain Maxwell equations and boundary conditions into the loss function, the method accurately predicts scattered fields across various dielectric configurations. A hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function was introduced to overcome singularities caused by sharp dielectric variations, achieving results comparable to finite-difference time-domain methods.

articles.title_original: Nematic phase transitions in Bernal bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Nematic Phase Transitions in Bernal Bilayer Graphene
articles.summary_en: Recent academic research explores nematic phase transitions in Bernal bilayer graphene, offering new physical insights into the electronic behavior and correlated states of two-dimensional carbon materials. articles.title_original: Microstructural design strategies for graphene-based flexible sensor conductors
articles.title_en: Microstructural Design Strategies for Graphene-Based Flexible Sensor Conductors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene-based flexible conductors represent a promising platform for multifunctional sensing applications, enabling simultaneous detection of temperature, humidity, and mechanical stress to meet the complex requirements of wearable electronics. The sensitivity and performance of these sensors can be significantly enhanced through strategic microstructural engineering of both the flexible substrate and conductive active layers. Various micro-nano architectures, including micro-domes, pillar arrays, cones, and bio-inspired structures, have been demonstrated to modulate sensing performance parameters. Unlike previous reviews that focused primarily on material synthesis or device fabrication, this review for the first time establishes a quantitative structure–performance relationship linking microstructural geometric parameters (i.e. aspect ratio, spacing, hierarchy) to sensor performance metrics (e.g. sensitivity, response time, detection range, durability). This review systematically examines the relationship between microstructural design and sensor performance, analyzing how geometric features influence sensitivity, response time, durability, and detection range. Compared with traditional conductive fillers such as silver nanowires, graphene offers superior structural flexibility and compatibility with micro-pattern processing. This review also briefly examines graphene/silver-nanowire composite structures as an emerging strategy for balancing conductivity and cost. By correlating structural characteristics with functional properties, we aim to provide design guidelines for optimizing graphene-based flexible sensors and establish a framework for developing next-generation multifunctional sensing systems.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines micro-nano architectural strategies for graphene-based flexible conductors used in multifunctional wearable sensors. It establishes a quantitative structure-performance relationship connecting geometric parameters like aspect ratio and spacing to sensor metrics including sensitivity, response time, and durability. The study provides design guidelines for optimizing next-generation sensing systems and compares graphene with silver-nanowire composite structures.

articles.title_original: Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers
articles.title_en: Fluctuation Electrodynamics of Quantum Capacitance in Electron Bilayers
articles.excerpt_original: Capacitance is a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons: it measures the energy cost of moving charge between conductors, and in low-dimensional systems this cost is shaped by exchange and correlation as much as by electrostatics. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form, with a universal coefficient; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the exact high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers follow the electron-gas template, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and reverses its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a theoretical framework for the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells, and graphene devices, focusing on interlayer correlations and van der Waals energy contributions. The study reveals that bilayer graphene exhibits anomalous interband screening that suppresses and reverses the sign of the quantum capacitance correction compared to standard electron-gas templates. This work demonstrates how quantum capacitance can probe interlayer pairing and coupled plasmon fluctuations in low-dimensional systems.

Graphene composites stand out among anode modification strategies due to their good conductivity and flexibility. They have been applied to silicon, sulfide, and oxide anodes. articles.summary_en: This academic review examines recent advancements in applying graphene composites to modify lithium-ion battery anodes, including silicon, sulfide, and oxide systems. articles.title_original: Thermoelectrically cooled Helmet with graphene-fabric composite liner for thermal management
articles.title_en: Thermoelectrically Cooled Helmet Utilizing Graphene-Fabric Composite Liner for Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Helmets are key parts of personal protective equipment (PPE) for workers and first responders in extreme environments. However, the metabolic heat generated by the head can accumulate within the helmet space, thus increasing the risk of heat stress in humans. This study presents a cooling helmet prototype that combines active thermoelectric cooling with a graphene-fabric composite liner. The prototype integrates a commercial thermoelectric cooler (TEC) with a graphene-fabric composite liner that functions as a heat spreader inside the helmet. Owing to graphene's high in-plane thermal conductivity, the liner spreads localized cooling from the TEC over a larger area, while the fabric substrate improves conformability and wearability. An incandescent bulb was used as a controlled and repeatable internal heat source, and the thermal responses were characterized using thermocouples and infrared thermography. In the transient heat-spreading test, under simultaneous heating and cooling, the liner temperature decreased by ~2.7 °C within 15 min and was approximately 5.2 °C lower than the heating-only condition. Infrared images showed that the graphene-fabric composite liner expanded the cooling-affected area to more than 12 times that of the TEC alone. Long-duration and climate-chamber tests further confirmed localized cooling near the TEC source and enhanced lateral cooling spread throughout the thermally conductive interlayers. Although the selected commercial TEC cooling capacity, along with the interfacial thermal resistance, slightly limited the overall performance, the results demonstrated the feasibility of using a TEC-assisted graphene-fabric heat-spreading liner for helmet thermal management and identified key directions for future optimization.
articles.summary_en: This academic study presents a prototype cooling helmet combining active thermoelectric cooling with a graphene-fabric composite liner acting as a heat spreader. Utilizing graphene's high in-plane thermal conductivity, the liner successfully distributes localized cooling over a significantly larger area inside the helmet. Testing under simulated heat sources demonstrated enhanced thermal management and reduced temperatures, proving the feasibility of the concept for personal protective equipment.

articles.title_original: Cavitation-Free Shear Emulsification Breaks the Yield–Damage Trade-Off in MXene Delamination
articles.title_en: Cavitation-Free Shear Emulsification for Low-Damage MXene Delamination
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The production of high-quality monolayer MXene nanosheets is constrained by the trade-off between delamination efficiency and structural damage. Here, we report a cavitation-free, high-speed shear emulsification strategy for the rapid, low-damage delamination of multilayer Ti3C2Tx MXene. Continuous fluid shear promotes interlayer sliding and separation, enabling an 82% monolayer yield within 10 min while retaining an average lateral size of approximately 5 μm and a film conductivity of 10,800 S cm–1, outperforming conventional ultrasonic delamination. Structural and spectroscopic analyses show that crystallinity and surface terminations are retained, enabling assembly into dense lamellar films. These films exhibit electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding effectiveness above 60 dB and an infrared emissivity of 0.11. Furthermore, the process is readily scalable to hundred-gram-level delamination, highlighting its potential for the large-scale production of high-quality MXene for multifunctional applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a cavitation-free, high-speed shear emulsification method to delaminate multilayer Ti3C2Tx MXene with minimal structural damage. The technique achieves an 82 percent monolayer yield within 10 minutes while preserving large lateral flake sizes, high electrical conductivity, and strong electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness. This scalable approach overcomes traditional yield-damage trade-offs in two-dimensional nanomaterial processing.

articles.title_original: High efficiency gold extraction by 2D metallic 1T/1T′ phase transition metal dichalcogenides
articles.title_en: High Efficiency Gold Extraction Using 2D Metallic Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
articles.excerpt_original: Recovery of precious metals from waste has high social and economic value, but in practice, recycling is often inefficient due to limits in technologies and materials. Here we show a group of materials—two-dimensional (2D) metallic 1 T/1 T′ phase transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs, MoS2, WS2, TaS2, and TiS2)—that allows for efficient, selective, and scalable extraction of valuable gold (Au) from leaching solutions of end-of-life electronics. The materials exhibit rapid kinetics, delivering an impressive 99.99% extraction efficiency of Au3+ in merely 0.25 min. Furthermore, they showcase strong selectivity for Au3+ adsorption, featuring a distribution coefficient (Kd) 5-6 orders of magnitude higher than that of other competitive cations (Cu2+, K+, Ni2+, Na+, Zn2+, Ca2+, and Mg2+). Amongst, TiS2 exhibits an unprecedented extraction capacity of 9093 mg⋅g−1 toward Au3+, which is approximately 1 order of magnitude higher than most other benchmark adsorbents (silver-organic frameworks). Importantly, through batch production of TiS2 nanosheets (5 g) and subsequent membranes fabrication for gold extraction, we demonstrated 0.15 g gold (23.8 Karat) recovery by treating 30 discarded central processing units (CPUs). Our work provides a foundation for the efficient and selective recovery of high-value metals from waste, contributing to a sustainable and circular economy. The authors demonstrate that metallic 2D transition metal dichalcogenides preferentially adsorb Au3+ and selectively reduce it to metallic gold, enabling efficient gold recovery from practical e-waste.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that two-dimensional metallic 1T/1T' phase transition metal dichalcogenides, such as TiS2 and MoS2, enable rapid, selective, and scalable extraction of gold from electronic waste leaching solutions. The materials achieve up to 99.99% extraction efficiency and high selectivity for Au3+ ions, offering a scalable pathway for precious metal recovery from discarded CPUs. This academic study contributes to sustainable e-waste recycling and circular economy technologies.
