articles.title_original: Flat-band formation and chiral superconductivity in driven topological insulators
articles.title_en: Flat-Band Formation and Chiral Superconductivity in Driven Topological Insulators
articles.excerpt_original: We demonstrate that circularly polarized light can be used to Floquet-engineer nearly flat or Mexican-hat like electronic bands on the surface of three-dimensional topological insulators (3D TIs), which under suitable conditions, can support topological superconductivity via purely repulsive Coulomb interactions. The driving acts not merely by gapping out the Dirac cone on the surface of the 3D TI, but can be used to diminish, and even flip in sign, the intrinsic curvature of the surface state dispersion away from the Dirac point. Using parameters for canonical 3D TIs, we find that the flat band limit is attained for reasonable electric fields and the bands realized by changing the strength of the driving field have a similar energetic and spatial profile to those obtained in rhombohedral graphene under varying displacement field, where the case for superconductivity with purely repulsive interactions has recently been made. We find that, with the aid of appropriately placed screening metallic gate, one can obtain $T_c \sim 7 $K in this setup while avoiding Wigner crystallization for low electron densities in the range of $10^{11}-10^{12}/\text{cm}^2$.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that circularly polarized light can Floquet-engineer nearly flat electronic bands on the surface of three-dimensional topological insulators. These engineered bands share spatial profiles with rhombohedral graphene systems, potentially supporting topological superconductivity with repulsive Coulomb interactions and critical temperatures around 7K.

articles.title_original: Graphene-based Hemispherical Transmitarray Antenna for Wide-Angle Beam Steering and Ultrafast Moving Target Tracking
articles.title_en: Graphene-Based Hemispherical Transmitarray Antenna for Wide-Angle Beam Steering
articles.excerpt_original: This work expands the application of dynamically tunable graphene to implement a hemispherical transmitarray antenna tailored for wide-angle electronic beam steering and ultrafast moving-target tracking at 250 GHz. The proposed hemispherical transmitarray antenna features a dynamically reconfigurable graphene-based multilayer configuration consisting of gold radiating patches, biased graphene sectors, hBN dielectric layers, and a centrally positioned hornfeed. The analytical framework of graphene-based reconfigurable metasurfaces including graphene surface-conductivity modeling, voltage-controlled surface impedance, transmission-coefficient, and conformal array-factor analysis, has been established for hemispherical transmitarray antenna for the first time. Moreover, the analytical and practical mapping between desired beam directions and the corresponding graphene bias voltages have been developed for the transmitarray antenna for the first time. Our transmitarray antenna possesses exceptional 3D beamsteering, providing wide-angle elevation scanning from -87 degrees to 87 degrees and full 360-degree azimuthal coverage. It also exhibits an antenna efficiency ranging from 68% to 80% with a 10% degradation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a dynamically tunable graphene-based hemispherical transmitarray antenna operating at 250 GHz for wide-angle electronic beam steering and ultrafast target tracking. articles.title_original: Majorana current induced by charge current in Kitaev magnet/graphene bilayers
articles.title_en: Majorana current induced by charge current in Kitaev magnet/graphene bilayers

We calculate Majorana current density based on the perturbation with respect to a Kondo type Majorana-electron coupling and obtain an analytical expression of the Majorana current induced by charge current, indicative of electronic control of charge-neutral Majorana fermions. We also discuss Majorana heat current induced by charge current and give estimations of their magnitudes.

The work also explores the associated Majorana heat current and provides theoretical estimations of its magnitude.

articles.title_original: Twisted Multilayer Graphene: Superperiodicity and quasicrystals
articles.title_en: Twisted Multilayer Graphene: Superperiodicity and Quasicrystals
articles.excerpt_original: This thesis investigates how superperiodicity, quasiperiodicity, and disorder shape electronic and spin transport in graphene-based systems, with an emphasis on experimentally relevant length scales and realistic atomistic modeling. Using large-scale real-space quantum-transport methods, it first establishes controlled transport fingerprints that distinguish conventional Bloch propagation in periodic structures from the anomalous dynamics induced by quasiperiodic modulations. Building on this framework, the thesis analyzes magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and shows that, within a finite disorder window where flat-band features remain robust, moderate Anderson disorder can counterintuitively enhance the mean free path. This disorder-induced delocalization is further linked to changes in the quantum metric extracted from optical conductivity, revealing a direct connection between transport, electronic geometry, and the real-space extent of the underlying states. The study then turns to graphene quasicrystal approximants and hybrid multilayer stacks, identifying sub-ballistic transport and self-similar localization patterns as signatures of quasicrystalline order, while also demonstrating their strong fragility against disorder and interlayer proximity effects. Finally, the thesis addresses spin transport in suspended monolayer graphene, showing that atomic-scale corrugations generate short-range fluctuating Rashba fields that can limit spin lifetimes to the nanosecond range even when charge transport remains close to ballistic. Taken together, these results provide a unified picture of how geometry, disorder, and structural complexity govern transport phenomena in twisted and corrugated graphene systems.
articles.summary_en: This thesis investigates electronic and spin transport in twisted multilayer graphene systems, exploring how superperiodicity, quasiperiodicity, and disorder affect transport properties. Using large-scale real-space quantum-transport methods, the study analyzes magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, graphene quasicrystals, and suspended monolayer graphene. The findings reveal mechanisms such as disorder-induced delocalization and the impact of fluctuating Rashba fields on spin lifetimes.

articles.title_original: Application of Graphene Separator in Different Battery Systems
articles.title_en: Application of Graphene Separators in Various Battery Systems
articles.excerpt_original: The rapid development of the new energy industry has raised higher demands on battery safety and energy density. As a physical barrier between the positive and negative electrodes, the diaphragm's performance directly determines the batteries’ cyclic lifespan and safety margins. The current commercial diaphragms have obvious deficiencies in thermal stability, electrolyte wettability, and mechanical strength. Graphene, with its two-dimensional layered structure, high mechanical strength, and excellent thermal stability, has become a research hotspot for modified membranes. This article outlines the mechanism of action and application progress of graphene-modified separators in different battery systems. In lithium-ion batteries, a graphene coating can enhance the thermal stability and ion conductivity of the separator, thereby improving the battery's cycling performance and safety. In lithium metal batteries, using heteroatom-doped or surface-functionalized graphene separators can effectively inhibit lithium dendrite growth and improve coulombic efficiency. In lithium-sulfur batteries, the graphene functional layer effectively alleviates capacity degradation caused by the shuttle effect through the synergistic action of physical sieving, chemical adsorption, and catalytic transformation. The article finally points out the main bottlenecks currently faced in this field and the directions for future research.
articles.summary_en: This academic paper reviews the application and mechanisms of graphene-modified separators across different battery systems, including lithium-ion, lithium metal, and lithium-sulfur batteries. It highlights how graphene coatings enhance thermal stability, inhibit lithium dendrite growth, and mitigate the shuttle effect to improve overall safety and cyclability. The article concludes by discussing current technical bottlenecks and future research directions in this field.

articles.title_original: Aharonov-Casher phase in twisted bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Aharonov-Casher phase study in twisted bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The Aharonov-Casher (AC) effect is a quantum mechanical phenomenon in which the wave function of a particle with a magnetic moment moving in a region subject to an electric field develops a phase shift due to spin-orbit interaction, even if no classical force acts on it. This phase also depends on the medium through which the particle moves. Here we focus on the AC phase of an electron moving in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) lying in the $x$-$y$ plane, subject to a uniform electric field perpendicular to the plane of the graphene, ${\bf E}=E{\hat{\bf z}}$. The AC phase is determined by an $SU(2)$ vector potential ${\bf A}$ from which a phase factor is generated, and used to perform a gauge transformation of the Hamiltonian. We find that the AC phase for a straight line path between two points in the TBG plane is linear with $E$ and exhibits sharp peaks at the magic angles. To help demonstrate an experimental method for determining the AC phase, we examine the probability of polarized electron propagation from a source tip to a drain tip in a double-tip scanning tunneling spectroscopy configuration.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigate the Aharonov-Casher effect for electrons moving in twisted bilayer graphene under a uniform electric field. The study finds that the phase shift is linear with the electric field and exhibits sharp peaks at magic angles, evaluated via a double-tip scanning tunneling spectroscopy configuration.

articles.title_original: Quantum oscillation spectroscopy of Fermi-surface topologies in tetralayer graphene
articles.title_en: Quantum Oscillation Spectroscopy Maps Fermi-Surface Topologies in Tetralayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Quantum oscillations offer a direct probe of Fermi-surface topology and electronic degeneracy, yet disentangling both simultaneously across the Lifshitz transitions of multiband systems has remained an open experimental challenge. Here, we use Shubnikov-de Haas spectroscopy on a high-mobility, dual-gated Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene (B-4LG) device to quantitatively reconstruct the complete sequence of six distinct Fermi-surface topologies-gully, annular, singly connected, and multiband pockets. The extracted oscillation frequencies determine the extremal momentum-space areas and their spin, valley, and gully-resolved degeneracies, in quantitative agreement with our tight-binding calculations. We further show that a perpendicular magnetic-field, combined with displacement-field lifts the valley degeneracy through an orbital-Zeeman coupling, producing a single-particle valley splitting of several $meV$, far larger than in bilayer or trilayer graphene. Our work demonstrates a framework for tracking Fermi-surface topologies and their flavor degeneracies in multiband quantum materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers utilize Shubnikov-de Haas spectroscopy on high-mobility, dual-gated Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene devices to reconstruct six distinct Fermi-surface topologies. The study details how perpendicular magnetic and displacement fields lift valley degeneracy via orbital-Zeeman coupling, yielding single-particle valley splittings significantly larger than those observed in bilayer or trilayer structures. This work establishes a quantitative framework for analyzing multiband quantum materials and their complex flavor degeneracies.

articles.title_original: MXene Bioinks for 3D Bioprinting: Design and Translation
articles.title_en: MXene Bioinks for 3D Bioprinting: Design and Translation
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXenes have emerged as electrically conductive, hydrophilic two‐dimensional nanomaterials uniquely suited for electroactive bioink development. However, the field lacks an integrated design framework that links MXene surface chemistry and colloidal behavior to printability, electrical percolation, and tissue‐specific biological outcomes. This review establishes a structure rheology biofunction paradigm for MXene‐based bioinks, critically examining how synthesis routes, surface terminations, and oxidation dynamics influence shear‐thinning behavior, network formation, and cytocompatibility. We analyze mechanistic pathways underlying cell–material interactions, including electrically mediated signaling and mechanotransduction in three‐dimensional constructs. Emerging in vivo studies are evaluated with emphasis on biodistribution, immune modulation, and long‐term biodegradation. Finally, we define key translational bottlenecks, oxidative instability, reproducibility, sterilization sensitivity, and regulatory classification, and propose actionable design criteria to advance MXene bioinks from laboratory constructs to clinically viable electroactive scaffolds.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines the integration of MXene nanomaterials into electrically conductive bioinks for 3D bioprinting. It proposes a structure-rheology-biofunction framework linking surface chemistry to printability, cell signaling, and in vivo biocompatibility. The study also outlines key translational challenges such as oxidative instability and sterilization sensitivity to guide clinical development.

articles.title_original: Optoelectronic Properties and Applications of MXene Quantum Dots
articles.title_en: Optoelectronic Properties and Applications of MXene Quantum Dots
articles.excerpt_original: MXene quantum dots (MQDs), as an emerging class of zero-dimensional nanomaterials, possess the quantum confinement effect, tunable bandgap structure, and excellent optoelectronic properties. It shows broad application prospects in fields such as sensing detection, biomedicine, optoelectronic devices, and energy and environment. This article systematically reviews the crystal structure, surface functional group characteristics, and size effect of MQDs. The mainstream preparation methods, such as hydrothermal/solvent thermal treatment, were introduced. The optical properties, such as ultraviolet-visible light absorption, tunable fluorescence emission, and nonlinear optical response, as well as key photovoltaic performances such as photoelectric conversion, photothermal effect, and carrier transport, were systematically investigated. The paper mainly elaborates on the application progress of MQDs in fields such as fluorescence sensing, biological imaging and diagnosis, photodetectors, photocatalysis, and energy storage. This article analyzes the prominent challenges currently faced by MXene quantum dots and looks forward to their future directions, which can provide a systematic reference for the basic research and engineering application of MQDs.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines the crystal structure, preparation methods, and optoelectronic properties of MXene quantum dots (MQDs). It highlights their applications in fluorescence sensing, biological imaging, photodetectors, photocatalysis, and energy storage. Furthermore, the paper discusses current challenges and outlines future research directions for MQD engineering.

articles.title_original: Thermodynamic principles governing MXene formation by molten salt etching
articles.title_en: Thermodynamic Principles Governing MXene Formation by Molten Salt Etching
articles.excerpt_original: Controlled reactions between MAX phases and molten salts allow selective A-element substitution or full A-element removal, providing a versatile route to both new MAX phases and two-dimensional (2D) MXenes. Despite its success, the broader applicability of this strategy remains limited, and the predictive power of theoretical approaches has not been systematically established. We recently introduced a thermodynamic methodology based on process-specific phase diagrams to describe reactions of MAX phases in molten salts, demonstrated for a narrowly defined set of representative systems. Here, we generalize this framework by adopting a more inclusive description of competing reaction outcomes and assess its applicability across a broad chemical space comprising 14 MAX phases and 7 molten salts. The predictions are benchmarked against reported experimental data and complemented by new experiments on previously unexplored MAX–salt combinations, encompassing both MXene synthesis and reaction outcomes beyond A-element substitution and MXene formation. While idealized stoichiometric models capture many trends, we identify experimentally relevant cases where non-ideal features – particularly non-stoichiometric A-element substitution and reduced termination occupancy – are required for quantitative agreement. More broadly, analysis of thermodynamic trends across all MAX–salt combinations yields clear criteria under which MXene formation is highly likely. The resulting framework provides a validated basis for computational screening and is expected to guide molten-salt-driven exfoliation strategies toward new two-dimensional materials beyond the MXene family.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the thermodynamic principles governing MXene synthesis through molten salt etching of MAX phases. By generalizing a thermodynamic framework across 14 MAX phases and 7 molten salts, the researchers establish reliable criteria for predicting MXene formation and other reaction outcomes. The findings offer a validated computational screening tool to guide the development of new two-dimensional materials.

articles.title_original: Preparation, Design, and Applications of MXene-Based Microwave Absorbing Composites
articles.title_en: Preparation, Design, and Applications of MXene-Based Microwave Absorbing Composites
articles.excerpt_original: With the rapid development of 5G/6G wireless communication technology, the issue of electromagnetic radiation pollution has become increasingly severe. The development of lightweight, thin, wideband, and high-efficiency microwave absorbing materials has become a major research focus. Transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXene), a class of two-dimensional materials, have garnered widespread research interest in electromagnetic wave absorption, benefiting from their high surface-to-volume ratio, superior metallic conductivity, and adjustable surface characteristics. This work provides a systematic review of the development of MXene fabrication methods, ranging from traditional fluorine-containing etching to eco-friendly fluorine-free routes, and elaborates on strategies to address impedance mismatch via covalent and non-covalent surface functionalization for tuning surface groups. The design strategies of two major optimization systems, namely magnetic material hybridization and dielectric material hybridization, are emphatically summarized. In addition, this paper summarizes the application status of in the fields of infrared stealth, thermal management, and supercapacitors, and analyzes the key issues existing in the current material systems. This review aims to provide a reference for the design and development of next-generation high-efficiency and intelligent MXene-based microwave absorbing devices, and points out that large-scale green preparation, enhanced oxidation resistance stability, and low-cost fabrication are the core research directions in the future.
articles.summary_en: This academic review discusses the synthesis, design strategies, and functional applications of MXene-based materials for electromagnetic wave absorption, infrared stealth, and thermal management. It highlights recent advancements in fluorine-free etching routes, surface functionalization, and hybridization with magnetic or dielectric components to address impedance mismatch. The study also outlines future research directions, emphasizing large-scale green production and improved oxidation stability.

articles.title_original: Recent Advances in the Applications of MXene Quantum-Dots for Biosensing
articles.title_en: Recent Advances in MXene Quantum Dots for Biosensing Applications
articles.excerpt_original: MXene quantum dots (MQDs) are a burgeoning novel material that stands out for its excellent physicochemical properties. It is especially effective in serving as biosensing materials. It can be utilized as a biomarker for health conditions or as a marker for remnant chemical composites. Recently, there have been a great deal of advancements in the development of MGDs. It is requisite to recapitulate the progress achieved, providing a systematic summary of recent developments. This paper systematically reviews the latest applications of MQDs in biosensing. MQDs are used to detect metabolites and disease biomarkers through electrochemical, conventional fluorescent, and ratiometric fluorescent strategies, enabling sensitive detection of all sorts of biomarkers. In addition, MQD-based fluorescent and ratiometric fluorescent sensors are applied to monitor environmental pollutants and food contaminants. Modification strategies, including elemental doping, noble metal loading, and nanocomposite superposition, significantly improve the sensitivity and selectivity of sensors. Despite remarkable progress, challenges including large-scale synthesis, biocompatibility, and device portability still exist. Refinement can be made, such as optimizing preparation methods, enhancing biocompatibility, and promoting clinical transformation. This review offers a thorough reference for the design and future development of MQD-based biosensors.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines the recent progress and applications of MXene quantum dots (MQDs) in biosensing, highlighting their utility in detecting disease biomarkers, environmental pollutants, and food contaminants through electrochemical and fluorescent strategies. It also discusses modification strategies to enhance sensitivity and selectivity, alongside ongoing challenges such as large-scale synthesis and biocompatibility.

articles.title_original: Multithiol Functionalized MXene Gel and Its Effective Adsorption Behavior for Cr(VI)
articles.title_en: Multithiol Functionalized MXene Gel for Effective Adsorption and Reduction of Cr(VI)
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) is a highly toxic heavy metal contaminant commonly used in industrial applications, posing significant risks to human health and environmental sustainability due to its persistence and difficulty in degradation. Transition metal carbide (MXene) is an emerging two‐dimensional material that has gained considerable attention for its potential in water pollutant removal. However, poor MXene stability and limited functional groups restrict its specific adsorption of target metal ions such as Cr(VI). Herein, a novel functionalized three‐dimensional MXene composite gel (M/D/P) was synthesized via a photo‐induced thiol‐ene click reaction using MXene as the framework material. The multithiol‐functionalized framework introduces abundant thiol groups, which facilitate the reduction of Cr(VI) to less toxic Cr(III) and enable chelation of Cr(III) with the adsorbent, driven by proton depletion during reduction. The adsorption behavior follows pseudo‐second‐order kinetics and the Langmuir model, indicating a chemical adsorption process. The maximum removal capacity reaches 347.71 mg·g − 1 , and the gel maintains 80% of its initial adsorption capacity after five cycles. The synergistic adsorption‐reduction mechanism, involving electrostatic attraction, reduction, covalent bonding, and chelation, highlights M/D/P as a promising MXene‐based adsorbent for water treatment applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have synthesized a novel multithiol-functionalized three-dimensional MXene composite gel designed for the removal of toxic hexavalent chromium from water. The material combines electrostatic attraction, chemical reduction from Cr(VI) to Cr(III), and chelation to achieve a high removal capacity. This study demonstrates the potential of functionalized 2D transition metal carbides in environmental remediation applications.

articles.title_original: Correction to “MXene‐Based Electromagnetic Attenuation Materials in Microwave and Terahertz Bands”
articles.title_en: Correction published for review on MXene-based electromagnetic attenuation materials
articles.excerpt_original: G. Zhang, S. Li, L. Chang, et al., “MXene-Based Electromagnetic Attenuation Materials in Microwave and Terahertz Bands,” Rare Metals 45, no. 2 (2026): e70079, https://doi.org/10.1002/rar2.70079. In the originally published version of this article, the equal authorship statement was inadvertently omitted. The correct author contribution information should include the following statement: “Guozheng Zhang, Sitong Li, and Libo Chang contributed equally to this work.” We apologize for this error.
articles.summary_en: This article provides a correction to a previously published study in Rare Metals regarding MXene-based electromagnetic attenuation materials for microwave and terahertz bands. The correction specifically addresses an omitted equal authorship statement involving the researchers. No new technical data or material developments are introduced.

articles.title_original: Surface coordination chemistry of MXenes: defects, terminations and anchored metal sites for inorganic redox catalysis
articles.title_en: Surface coordination chemistry and catalysis of MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes are usually reviewed as a broad family of two-dimensional carbides and nitrides, yet their most distinctive inorganic-chemistry feature is a dense, reactive and electronically coupled surface. This mini review frames MXenes as configurable coordination platforms rather than passive conductive supports. We discuss how terminal groups, metal vacancies, heteroatom substitution, interlayer ions, reconstruction and single-atom anchoring define local metal-ligand environments that regulate adsorption, charge transfer and catalytic selectivity. Representative examples from hydrogen evolution, oxygen electrocatalysis, single-atom-catalyst-mediated small-molecule redox chemistry, and rechargeable metal–air or lithium–oxygen chemistry are integrated with foundational studies on synthesis and surface characterization. The central message is that progress depends less on adding more components to MXene hybrids than on specifying which inorganic site is responsible for the reaction and how that site evolves under operating potentials.
articles.summary_en: This mini-review examines the surface coordination chemistry of MXenes, focusing on how terminal groups, defects, and single-atom anchoring regulate adsorption and charge transfer for inorganic redox catalysis. The study integrates findings from hydrogen evolution, oxygen electrocatalysis, and rechargeable metal-air energy storage applications.

articles.title_original: From surface terminations to functional nanoarchitectures: a chemistry-first framework for stabilizing and programming MXenes
articles.title_en: Chemistry-first framework for stabilizing and programming MXene nanoarchitectures
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes combine metallic conductivity, solution processability, and chemically addressable surfaces, but the reactive interfaces that enable functionalization also accelerate oxidation, restacking, and property drift. This Mini Review develops a chemistry-first framework in which surface terminations, defects, adsorbates, and interlayer species are treated collectively as a coupled state variable rather than as independent descriptors. We link etching and delamination chemistry to termination populations and discuss the effects of water and oxygen on spatially heterogeneous degradation. We then examine how molecular ligands, polymers, inorganic phases, and mesoscale assembly modulate interfacial reactions and transport pathways. We organize recent studies according to a causal sequence: chemical intervention, nanoscale structural consequence, transport response, functional output, and failure mode. This sequence helps explain why nominally similar Ti 3 C 2 T x materials can exhibit divergent electrochemical, catalytic, sensing, mechanical, and electromagnetic behavior. We argue that further progress depends less on identifying isolated applications than on controlling and reporting the evolving interfacial state across synthesis, storage, processing, and operation. We propose testable design rules for termination-aware synthesis, kinetic stabilization, interface-selective assembly, and operando validation. This framework positions MXenes as programmable reactive nanoarchitectures and identifies reproducibility, scalable fluorine-lean chemistry, and state-resolved characterization as priorities for nanoscience.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines the surface chemistry, degradation pathways, and functional programming of MXenes through a coupled state-variable framework. It establishes design rules for termination-aware synthesis, kinetic stabilization, and interface-selective assembly to improve material reproducibility and performance across diverse applications. The study emphasizes the importance of controlling the evolving interfacial state from synthesis to operation.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Bridged MXene Aerogel with Vertically Aligned Channels for Solar Evaporation and Electromagnetic Interference Shielding
articles.title_en: Graphene-Bridged MXene Aerogel for Solar Evaporation and EMI Shielding
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Aerogels based on pliable nanomaterials hold great potential for diverse applications. Herein, a bifunctional reduced graphene oxide-bridged MXene (rGM) aerogel with vertically aligned channels is fabricated via a facile directional freezing and mild thermal annealing strategy. This architectural design effectively mitigates the restacking and oxidation issues of MXene while optimizing its synergistic performance for solar evaporation and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding. The rGM aerogel thereby exhibits exceptional sunlight absorption (~96.2%), superior wettability, and efficient photothermal conversion. As a solar evaporator, it achieves a high evaporation rate of 2.62 kg m−2 h−1 and an energy efficiency of 91.68% under 1 sun illumination. Moreover, the synergistic conductive loss and multiple internal reflections within the aerogel deliver an outstanding EMI shielding effectiveness of 35.67 dB in the X-band (8.2−12.4 GHz). This work provides a versatile strategy for designing advanced aerogels that integrate efficient solar-thermal conversion with high-performance EMI shielding, opening promising avenues for multifunctional aerogel materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a reduced graphene oxide-bridged MXene aerogel featuring vertically aligned channels using directional freezing and thermal annealing. The bifunctional material achieves a high solar evaporation rate of 2.62 kg m-2 h-1 with 91.68% energy efficiency alongside an EMI shielding effectiveness of 35.67 dB in the X-band. This design effectively mitigates MXene restacking and oxidation, offering potential for multifunctional environmental and electronic applications.

articles.title_original: Electrochemical Hydrogen Pumps Powered by In-situ Waste Heat Recovery and Enhanced by 3D MXene‑CNT Carriers
articles.title_en: Electrochemical Hydrogen Pumps Powered by Waste Heat and Enhanced with MXene-CNT Carriers
articles.excerpt_original: Electrochemical hydrogen pump (EHP) technology is promising for purifying industrial byproduct hydrogen (IBH), but low cost and high efficiency are key for practical use. This study recovers low‑temperature waste heat from IBH to power the EHP and constructs a high‑surface‑area support (3D MXene‑CNT) to boost the reaction rate. The wrinkled structure inhibits MXene stacking, increases specific surface area to 213.5 m<sup>2</sup> g<sup>-1</sup>, and CNTs form an efficient conductive network. Applied to both EHP and a thermally regenerative battery (TRB), Pt‑3D MXene‑CNT exhibits a large electrochemically active area and low overpotential. At 1 V, the EHP achieves a current density of 1.12 A cm<sup>-2</sup> (93.1% higher than Pt/C) and low decay over 80 h. In the TRB, 3D MXene‑CNT‑S delivers a peak power density of 86.6 W m<sup>-2</sup> and 89.6% capacity retention after 30 cycles. A coupled TRB‑driven EHP system is demonstrated, showing higher H<sub>2</sub> production rate and longer operation time. This work provides theoretical guidance for efficient, low‑cost IBH purification.
articles.summary_en: This academic study reports an electrochemical hydrogen pump (EHP) powered by recovered low-temperature waste heat and utilizing a 3D MXene-carbon nanotube (CNT) carrier to boost reaction rates. The wrinkled MXene structure combined with CNT conductive networks inhibits stacking and significantly improves surface area, leading to high current density and durability. When coupled with a thermally regenerative battery, the system demonstrates an enhanced hydrogen production rate for industrial byproduct hydrogen purification.

articles.title_original: Dipolar interlayer excitons in transition metal dichalcogenide alloy heterobilayers
articles.title_en: Dipolar Interlayer Excitons in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Alloy Heterobilayers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Interlayer excitons in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers possess a permanent electric dipole moment and long recombination lifetimes, making them a promising platform for exploring excitonic many-body physics. Here, we report dipolar interlayer excitons in a MoS <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mi/> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> Se <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mi/> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>0.6</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> /MoSe <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mi/> <mml:mn>2</mml:mn> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> heterobilayer encapsulated in hexagonal boron nitride. Low-temperature photoluminescence measurements reveal a distinct emission peak at <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mo>∼</mml:mo> </mml:mrow> <mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> eV, attributed to radiative recombination of interlayer excitons. The emission exhibits a blueshift with increasing excitation power, indicating repulsive dipole–dipole interactions. Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements uncover nanosecond-scale lifetimes, consistent with the spatial separation of electrons and holes across the two layers. These findings establish chalcogen-alloyed TMD heterobilayers as a versatile platform for engineering dipolar excitons and tuning excitonic interactions in van der Waals materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report the observation of dipolar interlayer excitons in a MoS1.4Se0.6/MoSe2 transition metal dichalcogenide alloy heterobilayer encapsulated in hexagonal boron nitride. Photoluminescence measurements demonstrate repulsive dipole-dipole interactions and nanosecond-scale recombination lifetimes. These findings establish chalcogen-alloyed TMD heterobilayers as a versatile platform for engineering dipolar excitons in van der Waals materials.

articles.title_original: Topology-Optimized Kirigami Design of Electrospun BNNS/PVA Composite Films for Flexible Electronics Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Topology-Optimized Kirigami Design of Electrospun BNNS/PVA Composite Films for Flexible Electronics Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Flexible electronics require thermal-management materials that can efficiently dissipate heat while maintaining mechanical compliance under deformation. In this study, a topology-optimized kirigami BNNS/PVA composite film was developed by combining boron nitride nanosheet incorporation, electrospinning, and thermo-mechanical topology optimization. The electrospun BNNS/PVA network enhanced the in-plane thermal conductivity from 0.19 to 4.63 W/(m·K), while the optimized kirigami architecture improved deformation accommodation by reducing elastic strain energy accumulation. The average temperature and total elastic strain energy were reduced from 86 °C to 53 °C and from 43 J to 11 J, respectively. The optimized structure achieved a maximum stress of 2.39 MPa and a maximum strain of 5.02% and reduced the steady-state temperature by up to 21.27 °C under identical heating conditions. Furthermore, in-plane thermal conductivity was maintained after 300 bending cycles, which provides an effective material–structure design strategy for flexible electronic thermal management applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a topology-optimized kirigami BNNS/PVA composite film combining boron nitride nanosheets and electrospinning for thermal management in flexible electronics. The material achieved an in-plane thermal conductivity of 4.63 W/(m·K) and significantly reduced both operating temperatures and elastic strain energy under mechanical deformation. Furthermore, the composite maintained its thermal conductivity after 300 bending cycles, offering a robust design strategy for deformable electronic applications.

articles.title_original: Pauli-limit violation and high-resolution two-fold symmetric superconductivity in the kagome superconductor CsV <sub>3</sub> Sb <sub>5</sub>
articles.title_en: Pauli-limit violation and two-fold symmetric superconductivity in kagome superconductor CsV3Sb5
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Kagome superconductors have attracted intense interest due to the presence of many intriguing orders, such as charge density wave, nematicity, pair density wave, and possible unconventional superconductivity. Here, we report a pronounced violation of the Pauli paramagnetic limit in thin flakes of the kagome superconductor CsV3Sb5. In in-plane magnetotransport measurements, the upper critical field reaches ~8 T at 200 mK, far exceeding the Pauli limit expected for a superconductor with a critical temperature of 2.8 K. Remarkably, despite the hexagonal crystal symmetry, the in-plane upper critical field exhibits a robust two-fold angular anisotropy resolved with high-resolution angle precision of 0.1°. These observations are naturally explained by spin-orbit-parity coupling in CsV3Sb5, which renormalizes the Zeeman response of Cooper pairs, enhancing the critical field and stabilizing a two-fold symmetric superconducting state. Our results establish CsV3Sb5 as a platform where kagome electronic structure intertwines with spin-orbit-parity-protected superconductivity.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a pronounced violation of the Pauli paramagnetic limit and a robust two-fold angular anisotropy in the in-plane upper critical field of thin flakes of the kagome superconductor CsV3Sb5. These phenomena are explained by spin-orbit-parity coupling that renormalizes the Zeeman response of Cooper pairs and stabilizes the superconducting state. The findings establish CsV3Sb5 as a material system where kagome electronic structures intersect with protected superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Radiation‐Matter Interaction in Chemical Vapor Deposition‐Grown Two‐Dimensional Tungsten Disulfide
articles.title_en: Radiation-Matter Interaction in CVD-Grown 2D Tungsten Disulfide
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (2D‐TMDs) have attracted immense interest due to their unique layer‐dependent physical properties and wide applicability in electronics, optoelectronics, and sensing devices. However, their response to high‐energy radiation, crucial for deployment in extreme environments, remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate the radiation‐matter interaction in chemical vapor deposition (CVD)‐grown tungsten disulfide (WS 2 ). The material is irradiated with varying doses of γ‐radiation ranging from 100 to 1000 Gy. The irradiated samples were systematically characterized using Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence (PL), X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), and magnetic measurements. The results reveal that γ‐irradiation induces pronounced reductions in PL intensity, noticeable Raman peak shifts, and emerging magnetic responses at intermediate doses (≈500 Gy), indicating defect generation and lattice distortion. These findings enhance the understanding of γ‐ray interactions with 2D semiconductors and suggest that controlled irradiation could serve as a viable approach for tailoring their structural and optical characteristics for advanced device applications.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the interaction of gamma radiation with chemical vapor deposition-grown two-dimensional tungsten disulfide (WS2) across doses ranging from 100 to 1000 Gy. Characterization via Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence, XPS, STEM, and magnetic measurements reveals that irradiation induces defect generation, lattice distortion, and emerging magnetic responses. These insights advance the understanding of 2D semiconductor behavior in extreme radiation environments for advanced device applications.

articles.title_original: AmplifyingPolarimetric Photoresponse through OrientedColloidal Quantum Wells and Interfacial Band Engineering in ReSe2 Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Amplifying Polarimetric Photoresponse via Colloidal Quantum Wells and ReSe2 Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Polarization-sensitive two-dimensional (2D) photodetectors are important for imaging, optical communication, and weak-signal recognition, yet their performance is often limited by the intrinsic anisotropy of the 2D semiconductor channel alone. Inspired by squid’s polarization-sensitive vision from ordered photonic platelets, where crystal orientation governs light’s polarization and appearance, we report a polarimetric photodetector by integrating face-down-oriented CdSe/ZnS colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) with 2D anisotropic ReSe2, followed by sulfur-ligand exchange to further optimize the interfacial energetics. The face-down assembly preserves the in-plane transition dipoles of CQWs at the film level, thereby enhancing polarization-selective light absorption, while sulfur-ligand exchange modifies the CQW band-edge positions and facilitates interfacial carrier extraction. As a result, the optimized face-down CQWs-S/ReSe2 device exhibits a dichroic ratio of 1.443, a polarization ratio of 27.57, a maximum responsivity of 2.3 A/W, and a rise time/decay time of 1.03/3.12 ms, together with improved specific detectivity of 4.56 × 1010 Jones and operational stability under the photoconductive effect at 635 nm. Spatially resolved photocurrent mapping further shows that the distinctive polarization-dependent photocurrent extends across the entire heterostructure channel, which is ascribed to the efficient type-II band alignment with appropriated band offsets between CQWs-S and ReSe2. These results demonstrate that combining orientationally ordered CQW films with ligand-engineered interfaces provides an effective route toward high-performance polarization-sensitive photodetectors to be used in polarized imaging and encrypted communication.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a high-performance polarimetric photodetector by integrating face-down-oriented CdSe/ZnS colloidal quantum wells with anisotropic ReSe2. The device utilizes sulfur-ligand exchange to optimize interfacial energetics and carrier extraction, achieving an improved polarization ratio and specific detectivity. This approach offers a promising pathway for advanced polarized imaging and optical communication applications.

articles.title_original: Molecularly EngineeredCrystalline Donor–acceptorLinear Conjugated Polymer for 2 D /2D HeterostructuresToward Efficient Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
articles.title_en: Molecularly Engineered Crystalline Donor-Acceptor Linear Conjugated Polymer for 2D/2D Heterostructures Toward Efficient Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Breaking through the structural limitations of linear conjugated polymers (LCPs) is critical for high-performance heterojunctions. Herein, we report the rational molecular engineering of a crystalline two-dimensional (2D) donor–acceptor (D–A) polymer, poly(4,7-dithienyl-2,1,3-benzothiadiazole) (PDB), addressing conventional polythiophenes’ amorphous/zero-dimensional (0D) drawbacks of poor charge transport and interfacial compatibility. PDB’s rigid D–A backbone (thiophene donors + benzothiadiazole acceptors) enforces high crystallinity and 2D sheet morphology, endowing enhanced π–π overlap, high charge mobility, and abundant binding sites. Capitalizing on this, we fabricate a 2D/2D PDB/ZnIn2S4 (ZIS, denoted as PZS) heterostructure via in situ growth of vertical ZIS nanosheets on PDB. ZIS’s intrinsic 2D morphology enables intimate atomic contact, while its suitable bandgap and favorable band alignment facilitate efficient interfacial charge transfer. Combined experimental and DFT studies collectively support a Type-II band alignment, enabling directional electron transfer with minimized resistance. Consequently, the optimized PZS heterostructure with 0.2 mg PDB loading (denoted as PZS-0.2) delivers a remarkable visible-light H2 evolution rate of 4.99 mmol g–1 h–1, representing a 26.3-fold and 5.1-fold enhancement over pristine PDB and ZIS, respectively. This work establishes a new paradigm for high-performance LCP-based heterojunctions by integrating molecularly engineered 2D D–A conjugated polymers with inorganic semiconductors, providing a versatile design principle for efficient solar-to-fuel conversion.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a crystalline two-dimensional donor-acceptor conjugated polymer, poly(4,7-dithienyl-2,1,3-benzothiadiazole) (PDB), to address the poor charge transport and interfacial compatibility of conventional polymers. By fabricating a 2D/2D PDB/ZnIn2S4 heterostructure via in situ growth, the system achieves a Type-II band alignment that significantly enhances visible-light hydrogen evolution rates. This work demonstrates a novel design principle for integrating 2D conjugated polymers with inorganic semiconductors for efficient solar-to-fuel conversion.

articles.title_original: Predicting the Slow Drift of Nuclear Spin Noise in Semiconductor Spin Qubits
articles.title_en: Predicting Slow Nuclear Spin Noise Drift in Semiconductor Spin Qubits
articles.excerpt_original: The dynamics of a nuclear spin bath generates magnetic noise that is a key contributor to the decoherence of electron spin qubits in electrostatically-defined quantum dots. In this paper, we extend the cluster correlation expansion (CCE) technique, which has proven useful for predicting solid-state qubit coherence times across various settings but is limited to shorter time scales, to incorporate stochastic treatments of cluster dynamics in order to efficiently predict slow drifting Overhauser fields over longer time scales. This approach combines quantum evolution with classical rate matrices to enable simulation across a wide range of temporal regimes required to simulate, for example, the long-time convergence of the ergodic $T_2^*$ from Ramsey experiments. Our methodology is validated against experimental data from various silicon spin qubit systems, demonstrating a strong agreement between simulation and measurement of Ramsey experiments presented in the form of $T_2^*$ versus averaging time, autocorrelation functions, as well as power spectral densities. Furthermore, we demonstrate significant back-action effects through modeling and experiment; specifically, the dynamics of the nuclear spin bath depends upon the electron spin occupation schedule. Finally, our modeling quantitatively predicts the benefits from compensating for the slow drift of Overhauser fields in qubit operations. articles.summary_en: Researchers extend the cluster correlation expansion technique by incorporating stochastic treatments of cluster dynamics to predict slow drifting Overhauser fields in semiconductor spin qubits over extended time scales. The methodology successfully models nuclear spin bath dynamics, back-action effects, and qubit coherence improvements under field compensation strategies. This academic study contributes to the fundamental understanding and operational optimization of semiconductor-based quantum computing systems.

articles.title_original: Molecular Design, Crystallization Control, and Photoelectric Performance Comparison of High Mobility Organic Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Review on Molecular Design, Crystallization Control, and Photoelectric Performance of High Mobility Organic Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: In recent years, organic semiconductors have shown broad application prospects in the fields of organic field effect transistor (OFET), organic photovoltaic (OPV), and organic light emitting devices (OLED) due to their adjustable molecular structure, flexible processing, and low cost. However, the contradiction between high mobility and excellent photoelectric performance is still the core problem restricting its development. Based on the research progress of typical organic semiconductor systems in recent years, this paper systematically analyzes the molecular design strategies, crystallization control methods, and the influence mechanism on photoelectric properties of high mobility organic semiconductors. In the theoretical part, the molecular structure characteristics, carrier transport mechanism, doping, and interface engineering principles of organic semiconductors are described. In the part of performance comparison, the mobility, luminous efficiency, and device performance of typical material systems are compared. According to previous studies, through molecular conjugate structure optimization, crystal orientation control and Interface Engineering collaborative design, the carrier mobility can be significantly improved and the photoelectric performance can be taken into account, which provides theoretical guidance for high-performance organic optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: This academic paper reviews the recent progress in organic semiconductors, focusing on molecular design strategies and crystallization control methods to overcome the tradeoff between high mobility and photoelectric performance. It covers structural optimization, carrier transport mechanisms, doping, and interface engineering principles for applications in OFETs, OPVs, and OLEDs.

articles.title_original: Multilayer Assembly of Perovskite Heterostructures via Colloidal Suspensions
articles.title_en: Multilayer Assembly of Perovskite Heterostructures via Colloidal Suspensions
articles.excerpt_original: Realizing multilayer stacks analogous to classical semiconductors with precise control over chemistry, composition, thickness, orientation, and epitaxy using solution-processing has remained a long-standing bottleneck. Here, we present a novel scalable solution-based strategy for the deterministic deposition of any perovskite layer onto an existing perovskite film, enabling multilayer perovskite heterostructures with comparable control. Our approach dissolves pre-synthesized perovskite crystals or precursor salts in a dissolving solvent, followed by dispersion into a miscible carrier solvent to form a metastable colloidal system that can be deposited without disturbing the underlying layer. This universal process enables architectures including 3D-on-3D, 2D|3D, 3D|2D, and more complex multilayers, while independently controlling composition, thickness, orientation, and interfaces. We further show that lattice parameter matching enables orientation control through solution-phase epitaxy. Integrating a formamidinium-rich 3D|2D stack (FA 0.9 Cs 0.1 PbI 3 |(3AMP)FA 2 Pb 3 I 10 ) into p-i-n solar cells increases efficiency from 24.2% to 26.0%, maintained for 2D layer thicknesses up to 80 nm, establishing a versatile platform for scalable semiconductor heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable solution-based strategy for depositing deterministic perovskite layers onto existing films to create complex multilayer heterostructures. The method utilizes metastable colloidal systems to deposit layers without disrupting underlying structures, enabling precise control over composition, thickness, and orientation. Integrating these 3D|2D stacks into p-i-n solar cells improved efficiency from 24.2% to 26.0%, establishing a versatile platform for semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: Engineering photoluminescence in MXene quantum dot–based 2D/0D hybrids: interfacial design, mechanisms, and applications
articles.title_en: Engineering Photoluminescence in MXene Quantum Dot-Based 2D/0D Hybrids
articles.excerpt_original: MXene quantum dot–based two-dimensional/zero-dimensional (2D/0D) hybrid systems have emerged as an interdisciplinary materials platform for regulating optical and photophysical behavior through rational interfacial design. By integrating atomically thin 2D materials with zero-dimensional MXene quantum dots (MQDs), these hybrids exploit dimensional complementarity and chemically tunable interfaces to modulate light–matter interactions at the nanoscale. This review provides a comprehensive overview of structural design principles, interfacial assembly strategies, and interface-mediated electronic interactions governing photoluminescence (PL) in 2D/0D MQD hybrids. Particular attention is given to the influence of MQD size, surface terminations, interfacial coverage, and local chemical environments on energy redistribution, charge regulation, and suppression of nonradiative recombination pathways. Rather than focusing solely on physical models, the discussion highlights how surface chemistry and interface structure collectively shape exciton behavior and emission efficiency. Recent experimental advances demonstrating tunable, broadband, and multiphoton-induced PL are summarized, together with key challenges related to chemical stability, interfacial uniformity, and scalable fabrication. Finally, future perspectives for integrating MQD hybrids into optoelectronic, sensing, and energy-related technologies are outlined, underscoring their potential as versatile and chemically adaptable light-emitting materials.
articles.summary_en: This review explores structural design principles, interfacial assembly strategies, and interface-mediated electronic interactions governing photoluminescence in 2D/0D MXene quantum dot hybrids. It highlights recent experimental advances demonstrating tunable, broadband, and multiphoton-induced photoluminescence while addressing key challenges such as chemical stability and scalable fabrication. The article outlines future perspectives for integrating these hybrids into optoelectronic, sensing, and energy-related technologies.

articles.title_original: Electronic Structure and Fast Neutron Direct-Conversion Detection in Organic-Inorganic Hybrid Perovskites
articles.title_en: Organic-Inorganic Hybrid Perovskites for Fast Neutron Direct-Conversion Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Traditional semiconductor neutron detectors improve neutron detection efficiency by covering organic materials as the neutron conversion layer. However, the injection efficiency of the recoil proton into the semiconductor detector is also affected by the scattering of the conversion layer itself. Here we report the hybrid perovskite MAPbBr<sub>3</sub> (MA=CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) material, which merges the converter and semiconductor together in atom-scale, as fast neutron direct conversion detector to achieve efficient recoil proton injection. This hybrid material has a hydrogen concentration of 2.87×10<sup>22</sup> n cm<sup>-3</sup> and μτ product of 4.49×10<sup>-3</sup> cm<sup>2</sup> V<sup>-1</sup>, combining the advantages of organic and inorganic materials. For two-dimensional (2D) perovskite materials, (PEA)<sub>2</sub>PbBr<sub>4</sub> (PEA=C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) has a higher hydrogen concentration. However, the carrier transport in the Z direction is hindered by its double quantum well structure. The MAPbBr<sub>3</sub> detectors achieved direct fast neutron detection and exhibited good response with a deuterium-tritium (D-T) mixed beams neutron generator. Further calculations shows that MAPbBr<sub>3</sub> exhibits self-repairing effect, and the existence of H-vacancy defects neither create deep-level defects nor significantly affect the interlayer band alignment. This work opens up a new strategy for high-efficiency fast neutron detectors from the perspective of organic and inorganic hybrid materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate the use of the hybrid perovskite material MAPbBr3 as a fast neutron direct-conversion detector by integrating the converter and semiconductor at an atomic scale. The material achieves efficient recoil proton injection and exhibits a self-repairing effect with favorable defect tolerance. This approach offers a new strategy for developing high-efficiency fast neutron detectors.

articles.title_original: Dirac Fermion Scattering and Pseudospin Polarization in Structurally Asymmetric Graphene Wormholes
articles.title_en: Quantum Transport and Pseudospin Polarization in Asymmetric Graphene Wormholes
articles.excerpt_original: We study the quantum transport of massless Dirac fermions through two asymptotically flat graphene sheets connected by a structurally asymmetric catenoid wormhole in $(2+1)$-dimensional curved spacetime. Analytic scattering basis functions are derived: Hankel functions of integer order (in the half-flux sector) in the flat sheets and Gauss hypergeometric functions in the curved throat. We construct a transfer matrix via piecewise numerical matching, verifying unitarity up to numerical precision. The transmission probability rises monotonically to unity at high energies. Global transmission exhibits mirror degeneracy under inversion of structural asymmetry, but local observables depend on incidence direction. The manifold's spin connection acts as a Hermitian coupling inducing an $A/B$ sublattice imbalance at the throat. Structural asymmetry induces a local pseudospin imbalance. A larger curvature radius enhances $P_z$ polarization via a larger geometric phase; abrupt incidence suppresses it. Sub-barrier modes exhibit a negative transmission phase time, compatible with Hartman-type wave-packet reshaping.
articles.summary_en: This academic study investigates the quantum transport of massless Dirac fermions through structurally asymmetric graphene wormholes connecting two flat sheets. Researchers derived analytic scattering basis functions and demonstrated that structural asymmetry induces local pseudospin polarization, with curvature radius enhancing polarization via geometric phase. The findings offer theoretical insights into charge transport and pseudospin dynamics in curved graphene spacetimes.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Role of Electron and Photon Dose in Stepwise Laser-Induced Complete Deoxygenation of Graphene Oxide Revealed by In-situ TEM
articles.title_en: Synergistic Role of Electron and Photon Dose in Stepwise Laser-Induced Complete Deoxygenation of Graphene Oxide
articles.excerpt_original: Laser-induced reduction of graphene oxide (GO) represents a highly promising route to graphene synthesis, offering spatially localized processing, elimination of hazardous chemical reagents, and compatibility with ambient conditions. Here, we introduce a stepwise laser reduction strategy employing a 532 nm pulsed laser, monitored in real-time by in situ dynamic transmission electron microscopy (DTEM). By systematically varying the pulse sequence and the cumulative photon and electron dose, complete deoxygenation of GO is achieved while preserving film integrity. Core-loss EELS confirms full removal of oxygen functional groups and restoration of the sp$^2$ graphitic network, evidenced by a $π^*-σ^*$ energy separation of 7.0 eV, in close agreement with graphite (7.1 eV). Crucially, the cumulative electron dose is identified as an active parameter governing the reduction mechanism: electron beam exposure accounts for approximately 5 at. % of the initial oxygen removal and synergistically lowers the energy barrier for subsequent laser-driven deoxygenation, while excessive electron exposure compromises film integrity through crack formation. The optimal configuration achieves complete deoxygenation at a cumulative photon dose of 2.5 x 10$^3$ mJ/cm$^2$ with superior in-plane crystallographic order and minimal beam-induced thinning. This work establishes a versatile multi-parameter strategy for controlled scalable graphene synthesis via combined electron beam and laser irradiation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a stepwise laser reduction strategy using a 532 nm pulsed laser monitored by in situ dynamic transmission electron microscopy to achieve complete deoxygenation of graphene oxide. The study reveals that the cumulative electron dose synergistically lowers the energy barrier for subsequent laser-driven deoxygenation while restoring the sp2 graphitic network. This multi-parameter approach offers a controlled pathway for scalable graphene synthesis.

articles.title_original: First-Principles Wannier Representation of Proximity Effects
articles.title_en: First-Principles Wannier Representation of Proximity Effects in Graphene Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Proximity effects in layered heterostructures are usually represented by static parameters fitted to first-principles bands, which discards the energy dependence of the virtual hybridization, the momentum transfer, and the spatial structure. We overcome this limitation by deriving a dynamical proximity operator $\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}';ω)$ directly from density functional theory, downfolding the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian of the heterostructure onto a fixed low-energy target Wannier subspace and reproducing its spectrum exactly within that subspace. The construction separates direct matrix elements from virtual hybridization through all remaining states. In graphene on hBN/Co(0001), virtual hybridization generates more than $99\%$ of the proximity exchange and gives it a resonant frequency dependence set by the Co $d$ states. In graphene/PtSe$_2$ it resolves a sublattice-selective intervalley coupling with a $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ charge modulation, and in graphene/WSe$_2$ a bond-resolved Rashba coupling of $0.24$~meV, against below $1$~$μ$eV for the direct projection alone. Our results expose the limitations of static projections and establish a fitting-free microscopic foundation for low-energy modeling, spin-relaxation theory, and transport calculations.
articles.summary_en: This academic study presents a fitting-free dynamical proximity operator derived directly from density functional theory to model proximity effects in layered graphene heterostructures. By downfolding the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, the research captures energy-dependent virtual hybridization and momentum transfer in systems such as graphene on hBN/Co(0001), graphene/PtSe2, and graphene/WSe2. The findings reveal the limitations of static parameters and establish a microscopic foundation for low-energy modeling, spin-relaxation theory, and transport calculations.

articles.title_original: Van Hove singularity-driven giant Nernst signal in twisted double bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Van Hove Singularity-Driven Giant Nernst Signal in Twisted Double Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Twisted graphene layers host van Hove singularities (vHSs), peaks in the electronic density of states, thought to drive exotic phases in moiré materials, but their effect on thermal transport has remained unclear. Here we show that vHSs in twisted double bilayer graphene (tDBLG) generate an unusually large Nernst signal-the transverse voltage produced by a longitudinal temperature gradient in a magnetic field. The pronounced Nernst peaks at the vHSs of the conduction and valence bands of tDBLG are tunable by an electric field with a maximum value of $\sim 40$ $μV K^{-1} T^{-1}$ at $\sim 1$ $K$, which is comparable to the best-known Nernst materials. Our theoretical calculations show that the large enhancement of the Nernst signal arises from the Lifshitz transitions around the vHSs. These findings establish the Nernst effect as a sensitive probe of Fermi-surface topology in moiré materials, and identify a universal thermoelectric signature of van Hove singularities.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that van Hove singularities in twisted double bilayer graphene generate an unusually large, tunable Nernst signal driven by Lifshitz transitions. The findings establish the Nernst effect as a sensitive probe of Fermi-surface topology in moiré materials, identifying a universal thermoelectric signature of van Hove singularities.

articles.title_original: Everything is a Spin: The Secret Lives of SU(2)
articles.title_en: Topological Engineering of Two-Component Degrees of Freedom in Graphene and Quantum Matter
articles.excerpt_original: Spin, pseudospin, valley, polarization, and other two-component degrees of freedom share the geometry of SU(2), yet their topological manifestations are usually discussed as separate phenomena. This review develops a common geometric language for their winding in momentum and real space,beginning with Berry phase and the Dirac Hamiltonian and extending to graphene, topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, and magnetic skyrmions. We argue that the common thread is not merely topology itself, but the continuity constraints imposed on two-component wavefunctions. Whenever the relevant symmetry is preserved, winding determines which states can continuously connect across an interface or deformation, thereby governing transmission, torque generation, optical selection rules, and other physical responses. We then ask a practical question: what does topology buy an engineer? In skyrmions, winding partitions magnetic configuration space and stabilizes ultrasmall information carriers with tunable dynamics. In graphene, pseudospin matching governs Klein tunneling, enabling a gate-controlled transmission gap without sacrificing the massless Dirac dispersion. In topological insulators and Weyl semimetals, spin-momentum locking and Berry-curvature engineering generate electrically selectable spin currents, while helicity-dependent optical transitions produce circular photogalvanic responses. Together, these examples suggest that topology is not merely a classification of quantum matter, but a design language in which symmetry-protected wavefunction continuity can be engineered for memory, switching, actuation, and sensing.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines the common geometric and topological principles governing two-component degrees of freedom such as spin, valley, and pseudospin across various quantum materials. Focusing on graphene, topological insulators, and Weyl semimetals, the study highlights how symmetry-protected wavefunction continuity and winding phenomena can be engineered to enable novel device applications in switching, sensing, and memory.

articles.title_original: Miniaturized broadband computational spectrometer based on graphene microelectromechanical system
articles.title_en: Miniaturized broadband computational spectrometer using graphene MEMS
articles.excerpt_original: Miniaturized spectrometers open new avenues for on-chip and portable optical sensing, with broad applications in fundamental research, biomedical analysis, and consumer electronics. Herein, we propose a miniaturized computational spectrometer framework based on a graphene microelectromechanical system (MEMS) Fabry–Pérot (FP) metal-cavity filter. By dynamically tuning the resonant peak wavelength of the FP cavity via the applied driving voltage, the spectral response of the graphene photodetector is calibrated for spectral encoding. Combined with an adaptive regularization algorithm, the proposed framework enables accurate spectral reconstruction. The computational reconstruction-based architecture broadens the operating bandwidth and enhances spectral resolution via its diverse multi-order spectral coding. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the miniaturized spectrometer features a micrometer-scale footprint, achieves a spectral resolution of 3.0 nm, and provides an operating bandwidth of 1.5 μm. Benefiting from the ultrahigh resonant frequency of the graphene-MEMS structure, the photocurrent sampling period of the photodetector is only 100 μs, endowing the spectrometer with submillisecond temporal resolution. This compact, high-performance scheme offers a feasible route toward integrable miniaturized spectrometers for next-generation industrial applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a miniaturized computational spectrometer framework driven by a graphene microelectromechanical system (MEMS) Fabry-Perot metal-cavity filter. The design utilizes dynamically tuned resonant peak wavelengths via applied voltages for spectral encoding and accurate reconstruction. Numerical simulations show the device achieves high spectral resolution, a wide operating bandwidth, and submillisecond temporal resolution.

articles.title_original: Ultra‐Robust (>700 K) Vacuum‐Ultraviolet Radiography Enabled by Nano‐Polycrystalline hBN
articles.title_en: Nano-Polycrystalline hBN Enables Ultra-Robust Vacuum-Ultraviolet Radiography
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT To address the urgent demand for high‐temperature vacuum‐ultraviolet (VUV) imaging detection in solar storm monitoring, this study develops a nano‐polycrystalline hexagonal boron nitride (NPhBN) scintillator with exceptional thermal robustness. Enabled by high‐temperature rapid chemical vapor deposition, wafer‐scale fabrication of an 8‐inch format is achieved. Its unique 2 nm grain structure simultaneously set records with a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 69.2% and an unprecedented thermal quenching temperature of up to 720 K with outstanding stability. VUV radiography at 523 K demonstrates that NPhBN maintains superior imaging quality under extreme conditions, effectively overcoming the thermal deactivation issue plaguing conventional scintillators in high‐temperature environments. Remarkably, NPhBN also exhibits outstanding VUV scintillation properties at room temperature, including an ultrafast decay time of 4.7 ns and a high spatial resolution of approximately 45 lp/mm. This work provides a robust VUV scintillator solution for solar disaster early‐warning systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers have developed a nano-polycrystalline hexagonal boron nitride scintillator using high-temperature rapid chemical vapor deposition, achieving wafer-scale 8-inch fabrication. The material demonstrates exceptional thermal robustness up to 720 K and high photoluminescence quantum yield, addressing critical needs in high-temperature vacuum-ultraviolet imaging for solar storm monitoring. Furthermore, it exhibits an ultrafast decay time of 4.7 ns and high spatial resolution at room temperature, offering a robust solution for extreme-environment disaster early-warning systems.

articles.title_original: A Catalogue of Topological Moiré Bands in Twisted Semiconductors
articles.title_en: High-Throughput Discovery and Classification of Topological Moiré Bands in Twisted Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Twisted two-dimensional semiconductors provide a route to flat and topological moiré minibands, but systematic principles for organizing their material dependence have remained unclear. Here, we establish a high-throughput framework that integrates structural relaxation, first-principles electronic structure calculations, and moiré band topology. We apply this framework to 43 experimentally realized monolayers and 91 symmetry-inequivalent bilayer prototypes, yielding over 1,000 angle-resolved moiré electronic band structures. This database reveals that the low-energy moiré electronic structure is organized primarily by the valley character of the parent band edge together with stacking symmetry. In $Γ$-valley systems, the miniband width usually follows a nearly quadratic twist-angle scaling, consistent with a folding-dominated kinetic-energy scale. In $K$-valley systems, stacking-controlled interlayer hybridization governs whether parent Berry curvature is redistributed into isolated valley Chern minibands. By contrast, $M$-valley systems form a more material-specific class associated with anisotropic and symmetry-constrained band folding. The same valley-and-stacking hierarchy rationalizes the emergence or suppression of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ minibands, and surface termination in Janus bilayers provides a microscopic knob for changing the relevant valley character. These results establish a materials-level organizing principle for designing flat and topological moiré bands in twisted semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a high-throughput framework combining structural relaxation, first-principles calculations, and band topology to analyze twisted two-dimensional semiconductors. The resulting database of over 1,000 angle-resolved moiré band structures reveals that valley character and stacking symmetry govern the emergence of flat, topological, and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ minibands. These principles provide a systematic approach for engineering novel electronic behaviors in layered semiconductor systems.
